utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am the lead counsel, Dragoljub Djordjevic, and today together with me is co-counsel Mr. Djurdjic, and our three legal assistants, Mr. Aleksandar Popovic, Ms. Marie O'Leary, and Mr. Russell Hopkins. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Vlastimir Djordjevic and the Office of the Prosecutor lodged appeals against the trial judgement rendered in this case on the 23rd of February, 2011, by Trial Chamber II. In accordance with the Scheduling Order issued by me on the 22nd of March, 2013, the Appeals Chamber will hear the appeals in this case today. Before doing so, I will provide a brief summary of the case, as is customary, and of Mr. Djordjevic's and the Prosecution's respective grounds of appeal. I will then outline how we will proceed today. This case concerns the responsibility of Mr. Djordjevic for crimes committed by the forces of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and Serbia in Kosovo from 1st January to 20th June 1999. During this relevant period, Mr. Djordjevic was the assistant minister of the MUP, the Ministry of Internal Affairs of Serbia, and chief of the public security department. The Trial Chamber found that from at least early January to June 1999, a joint criminal enterprise, or as it may be referred to in the course of this hearing, JCE, existed amongst the political, military, and police leadership of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and Serbia, including Mr. Djordjevic himself. This JCE had the purpose of modifying the ethnic balance of Kosovo in order to ensure Serbian control over the province by waging a campaign of terror and violence against the Kosovo Albanian population, which included the commission of deportations, forcible transfers, murders, and persecutions. The Trial Chamber found that this campaign was carried out by Serbian forces, including numerous MUP forces under the command and control of Mr. Djordjevic. It further found that Mr. Djordjevic contributed to the joint criminal enterprise, inter alia, through his failure to investigate and active concealment of crimes committed against Kosovo Albanians. The Trial Chamber convicted Mr. Djordjevic pursuant to Article 7(1) of the Statute, on the basis of both commission through his participation in the JCE and for aiding and abetting the following crimes: Deportation; murder; other inhumane acts, consisting in forcible transfer; and persecutions on racial grounds, through deportation, forcible transfer, murder, and destruction or damage to property of cultural and religious significance, as crimes -- these as crimes against humanity under Article 5 of the Statute. In addition, was also convicted for murder as a violation of the laws or customs of war under Article 3 of the Statute. The Trial Chamber, however, found that persecutions through sexual assault had not been established. Mr. Djordjevic, as you are aware, was sentenced to 27 years' imprisonment. Mr. Djordjevic advances 19 grounds of appeal challenging his conviction and his sentence and requests that the Appeals Chamber reverse his convictions in their entirety or, in the alternative, reduce his sentence. In grounds one through eight, Mr. Djordjevic alleges a number of errors of law and fact with respect to the Trial Chamber's findings concerning the joint criminal enterprise. In grounds nine and ten, Mr. Djordjevic challenges the Trial Chamber's findings concerning his participation in the JCE and his mens rea for JCE liability. In ground 11, he challenges the Trial Chamber's conclusion that he aided and abetted the crimes. And in ground 12, he submits that the Trial Chamber erred in its determination of the protected status of individuals. In ground 13, he submits that the Trial Chamber erred in finding that a de facto border existed between Kosovo and Montenegro. In grounds 14 to 17, he alleges that the Trial Chamber committed several errors of law and fact in relation to its findings concerning the crimes of deportation, other inhumane acts consisting in forcible transfer, murder, and persecutions. In ground 18, Mr. Djordjevic challenges his conviction for the crimes on the basis of both joint criminal enterprise liability and aiding and abetting and the cumulative convictions entered by the Trial Chamber in relation to Article 5. Finally, in ground 19 Mr. Djordjevic challenges the sentence imposed on him by the Trial Chamber. The Prosecution responds that all grounds of Mr. Djordjevic's appeal should be dismissed. I will now turn to the appeal of the Prosecution. The Prosecution advances two grounds of appeal. Under its first ground, the Prosecution argues that the Trial Chamber erred in law and fact in finding that persecutions through sexual assault had not been established. Under its second ground of appeal, the Prosecution submits that the Trial Chamber erred in exercising its discretion in determining the sentence. Mr. Djordjevic responds that the Prosecution's grounds of appeal should be dismissed. During this hearing, counsel may argue the grounds of appeal in any order they consider suitable for their presentation. I recall that the parties were invited to discuss a number of issues set out in the addendum to the Scheduling Order issued on 12th April 2013. For the sake of clarity, I ask that the parties indicate which issue they are addressing by reading out the relevant question at the beginning of their submission. I also urge counsel not to repeat verbatim or to summarise extensively the arguments presented in their briefs with which, please remember, the Appeals Chamber is already familiar. I also stress that the parties are invited to provide precise references to material supporting their oral submissions. I would also like to recall that this appeal is not a trial de novo and the parties must refrain from repeating their cases which were presented at trial. Article 25 of the Statute stipulates that the parties must limit their arguments to any alleged errors of law which invalidate the trial judgement or alleged errors of fact which occasion a miscarriage of justice. I will now turn to the timetable for the submissions to be made by the parties today. On the 8th May, the Appeals Chamber issued an amendment to the aforementioned addendum, introducing a slight revision to the timetable for the parties' submissions. I take this opportunity to apologise to you all for the change on such a short notice; however, it was unavoidable and I wish to thank the parties for their co-operation and understanding. Basically, in the absence of the President later on today and as acting President, I have -- I've been charged with dealing with a high-level meeting with a delegation from one particular country in anticipation of a future event happening here in the Tribunal, and it was either the President or myself that could conduct it or preside over this meeting. So I had to arrange -- make arrangements to stop for one hour. The idea is the meeting may well take up a whole hour or it may well take up less time. In that case, I will ask you to stand by at least 15 to 30 minutes before we are supposed to re-start at 4.00 so that if we can start earlier, we will start earlier. But I will let you know in due course. In accordance with the amendment, we will proceed as follows. We will first hear the appeal submissions of Mr. Djordjevic. And counsel for Mr. Djordjevic, or whoever will be doing this, will have a total of two hours for their submissions. We will have a break after one hour and 20 minutes of Mr. Djordjevic's submission. We will then resume at 11.00 for the remainder of the submissions by counsel for Mr. Djordjevic. And then we will proceed immediately with the Prosecution's response. The Prosecution also will have two hours. We will then break for lunch at 12.40 and resume at 2.00. For the time being, I won't mention the rest of the timetable. That will come later. We will now move immediately to hear submissions by the Djordjevic team. Thank you. I wish to remind parties that we may interrupt them at any time to ask questions or may ask questions following each of their submission or at the end of the hearing depending on what we think is best at any given time. Thank you. I know that you will be standing up but while you remain seated I cannot see you. So if you could actually move -- later on when you're sitting, move one chair it will be better for everyone. So good morning and you are in control now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS

I want to thank you for granting our request to allow our legal assistants to present our submissions. Mr. Hopkins.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hopkins, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOPKINS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOPKINS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, members of the Prosecution and to everybody in and around the courtroom. Djordjevic is 64 years old. He, as you know, was convicted and sentenced to 27 years of imprisonment on the basis that no other surviving member of the JCE made a more crucial contribution to the achievement of its objective. There are, we would suggest, three central pillars to his JCE convictions. First, his overall position as chief of the RJB and an assistant minister of the interior; second, his role in the deployment of the Skorpions to Kosovo; and thirdly, his role concealing the bodies of Kosovo Albanians inside Serbia. You can see the Trial Chamber's particular reliance on those three things at paragraphs 2154 to 2156 of the judgement. We say that Djordjevic's liability for crimes in Kosovo has been overstated and his sentence is too harsh. In the course of our submissions this morning, we will criticise a number of legal and factual errors that the Trial Chamber made. We criticise in particular the metamorphosis that one sees, whereby earlier discussions of the evidence are summarised incorrectly and then used to support sweeping conclusions. Now, Djordjevic faced a circumstantial case from which the Trial Chamber inferred his mens rea and attributed crimes to him. Our submission on appeal is that other inferences existed about Djordjevic's role and his intent. The Trial Chamber reached conclusions of fact from the circumstances when those were not the only conclusions reasonably available. For that reason, you are entitled to intervene, just as the Appeals Chamber did in the recent Bizimungu appeal and the Gotovina appeal. In our submission, the answer to your first question illustrates why you should intervene. Now, we understand your first question to have two subparts. The first is how the areas of responsibility of assistant ministers Zekovic and Stevanovic overlapped and impacted Djordjevic's authority; the second part is about Djordjevic's role in the deployment of the Skorpions to Kosovo. Now, with your permission we will deal with the Skorpions first before turning to Zekovic and Stevanovic. Now, in the early morning of the 28th of March, 1999, the Skorpions massacred 14 women and children in Podujevo in the north of Kosovo. Now, there were of course other atrocities committed in Kosovo in 1999, but the Trial Chamber thought this one particularly important because Djordjevic was, it concluded, directly implicated in it. It is notable, we say, that the section of the judgement that deals with Djordjevic's overall role and knowledge is 54 pages long and the Skorpions takes up nearly half of that. So this is a vital part of the Trial Chamber's conclusion that Djordjevic was a member of the JCE. Now, we will ask you to cast a critical eye over paragraph 2155 of the judgement. And there, in the later section of the judgement, you see the Trial Chamber's ultimate conclusion that Djordjevic participated in the JCE, based on points that it considered to have been established by its earlier discussion. Now, we again say, and this is not an uncommon feature in the judgement, you see in paragraph 2155 a metamorphosis, whereby earlier findings are summarised incorrectly and then used to support flawed conclusions. Now, with that introduction, we will answer your question in three stages. And if I may just a brief housekeeping matter. I envisage spending about 20 minutes or so on the Skorpions and then another 20 minutes or so on the assistant ministers, so 40 minutes on your first question. The three stages that we propose to address your question on the Skorpions through is, firstly, the circumstances of the initial deployment of the Skorpions to Kosovo; secondly, Djordjevic's role in their recall from Podujevo after the killing there; and thirdly, the circumstances and Djordjevic's role of their redeployment to Kosovo in late April. Firstly, then, on their initial deployment, there are at least five ways that we say the Trial Chamber erred. Point one, the Chamber concluded at paragraphs 2155 and 2188 of the judgement that the Skorpions were widely known as a notorious paramilitary formation. Now, that is a finding that no reasonable Trial Chamber would have made. The earlier finding was that the Skorpions had committed crimes in Croatia and a massacre at Trnovo, Bosnia, in 1995. Now, you will all recognise Trnovo from the Popovic judgement, paragraphs 587 and 1080 of that case. Now, I don't want to give evidence, but it is, in our submission, common knowledge that the first time that this massacre emerged was during the Milosevic trial when a well-known video of it came to light. There is, we suggest, no clear basis that such things were widely known in 1999. Now, the Trial Chamber at paragraph 204 relied on the evidence of Vasiljevic, a VJ general who subsequently investigated the Skorpions. But all he said in his evidence at transcript page 5667 was that he later discovered that there were, he says, criminal types in their ranks, problematic people, in his words. He didn't say that they were -- that this was widely known beforehand. He did not say - and this is crucial - that this was known or should have been known to Djordjevic beforehand. Point two, the unit of reserve forces is referred to throughout the judgement as the Skorpions, but only 15 or 16 of the 128 were former Skorpions, that's 12 and a half per cent. Indeed, the Trial Chamber noted that only half of them had any previous combat experience, you see that at paragraphs 1937 and 1951. So how is it said that Djordjevic knew that any of these 15 or 16 former Skorpions had committed war crimes in Croatia or Bosnia? That is a key point that the Trial Chamber just doesn't address. Point three, background checks. Now, at paragraph 1953 of the judgement, the Trial Chamber makes a sort of fall-back finding that, well, Djordjevic should have at least emphasised the need to screen these people for their backgrounds, and two of the Skorpions, it turns out, had prior convictions in Croatia. But paragraph 1954 of the judgement reveals an approach again that no reasonable Trial Chamber would take. The last sentence of that paragraph disparages a perceived suggestion by a witness that prior convictions in Croatia, and it said, did not count. But if you look to the evidence cited, the Chamber mis-characterises what the witness actually said. He didn't say that convictions in Croatia did not count; rather, he said, and the transcript reference is 13716, which is two pages further on from the transcript pages that the trial judgement cites. "Q. Can the MUP ask for reports for records of convictions outside of the Republic of Serbia? "A. Only through the courts, otherwise it cannot." So the witness was saying that convictions in Croatia could not be easily discovered. A search by the MUP of its criminal records in Serbia would not show up a hit, if you like, for a conviction in Croatia or anywhere else for that matter. And paragraph 228 of our appeal brief cites evidence that suggests that background checks were indeed undertaken and came back clear. So this puts something of a different light on the recruitment and deployment of the Skorpions. And finally on this point about background checks, you will note that there is no finding in the judgement that any of the Skorpions had criminal convictions in Serbia. This, we say, is consistent with background checks being undertaken and cleared. No reasonable Trial Chamber could use this issue of background checks against Djordjevic. Point four, we say that the trial judgement persists in a sort of mantra that the Skorpions were paramilitaries, but they were not alongside police or military structures, they were in it. They were incorporated into the SAJ reserve forces and brought into its chain of command, so they weren't para anything. Now, in an ideal world, maybe no such recruitment would be undertaken, but the 24th of March, 1999, when these men were incorporated into the SAJ, plainly was not an ideal world. The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia faced a national emergency. Now, you might think that the rather rushed decision to incorporate these men is unattractive. But we say that in all the circumstances, considering the context, it was not criminal. Point five, where were these men sent and why? Podujevo was a key strategic zone. The only other two SAJ units, the Pristina SAJ and the Belgrade SAJ, were there too. Now, the Skorpions were not sent off to some soft target. Podujevo and the surrounding area was a known KLA stronghold. In the north of Kosovo, it sat on the main artery connecting Kosovo to the rest of Serbia. If Djordjevic wanted to kill or expel civilians, Podujevo is not an obvious target. So we have made five points about the initial deployment of the Skorpions. We move now on to our second area, the response. And again, we have five points. Firstly, the immediate aftermath of the atrocity. Serbian medical teams arrived there and tried to save lives and treat the wounded; see paragraphs 1253 and 1255 of the judgement. Other members of the SAJ assisted with this. Also, the SAJ commander on the ground informed Djordjevic in Belgrade. Telephones to Belgrade were still working on that day. The point we ask you to note at this stage is that Djordjevic finds out straight away. Point two, the withdrawal. The unit consisted of 128 men. Now, the Trial Chamber was unable to make a precise finding of the number involved in the massacre, but the evidence suggests that perhaps ten of the 128 men were directly involved. You see that in paragraphs 1248 and 1250 and the evidence cited there. It is uncontroversial, we would suggest, that Podujevo was committed by a small fraction of the overall unit. Yet, the entire unit was withdrawn, all 128 of them, straight away. They were recalled first to Prolom Banja, then Djordjevic ordered Trajkovic to go there to disarm them all and then sent them home, you see that at paragraph 1963. We say that this is not the action of somebody whose mens rea is as the Trial Chamber concluded. Point three, further action. On the morning of 30th of March, 1999, so two days later not three as the Trial Chamber suggests at one stage, an investigative judge travelled to Podujevo. He was told about this crime by the Podujevo OUP and he attends the crime site together with the police. His report is Exhibit D441. So the sequence is that Djordjevic finds out straight away. The OUP is involved immediately. People who, on the Prosecution's case, Djordjevic could order around, but - and this is a point we will return to - there is no cover-up. Instead, all of the bodies were buried properly in a local cemetery. See paragraph 1454 of the judgement, where it says that the bodies were buried in a line, each grave was marked with a piece of wood, and numbered consecutively. Point four, more action. On the 13th of May, following a request by Djordjevic, the overall commander of the SAJ submitted a report on this atrocity; that's Exhibit D442 and P86. Then on the 23rd of May, the Podujevo OUP filed a criminal report against people identified as the perpetrators. That's Exhibit P1593, which you can see was sent to the competent prosecutor. Now, the next day the prosecution filed a request to conduct further investigations and the investigative judge decided to proceed, that's Exhibit P1592 [Realtime transcript read in error "P1592"], following which two suspects were detained. The prosecutions continued, albeit slowly, and resulted in a judgement in April 2002. That's Exhibit P40, where somebody was convicted and got a 20-year sentence, the maximum available. By Exhibit P41 we can see that his appeal was dismissed. Point five, what about the suggestion at paragraph 1963 of the judgement that withdrawing the Skorpions hindered the investigation? That recalling them to Belgrade, disarming them, and sending them home somehow avoided prosecutions. No reasonable Trial Chamber would draw that conclusion. It is obviously contrary to the clear chain of events, and we refute the apparent suggestion in the trial judgement that the entire unit had to remain in Podujevo or Prolom Banja for the police to investigate. There can be no sensible suggestion that the people had to remain in Podujevo or the vicinity of the crime for the police or the prosecutor to have jurisdiction. And I'm told that I erroneously referred to Exhibit P159 a moment ago and it should have been Exhibit 1592. So we say this sequence in Podujevo contrasts from the Trial Chamber's conclusion at paragraph 1962 that the Trial Chamber says no person was prosecuted for the crimes in Podujevo. It's right that nobody had been convicted during Djordjevic's tenure as chief of the RJB, but the criminal proceedings were well underway. The process started on the 30th of March and Djordjevic plainly didn't stop it. So we have discussed the circumstances of the initial deployment and the response. Moving to our third and final area in relation to the Skorpions, their redeployment to Kosovo. Firstly, again of five points, 108 of the 128 were re-engaged by the SAJ. See paragraph 1945. So 15 per cent did not return to Kosovo. Those who took part in the atrocity in Podujevo were not deliberately redeployed. See paragraph 1946 where this point is noted in passing. Now, the Trial Chamber concluded at paragraph 1966 that some of those involved had been redeployed, but we say it is reasonably possible that that was not deliberate. And it seems undisputed that one of the main perpetrators of the crime in Podujevo, Sasa Cvetan, was not redeployed. Secondly, 85 per cent of the unit was only sent back to Kosovo on the 26th of April, so a whole month after Podujevo. Yet, there is no consideration by the Trial Chamber that if Djordjevic really was intent on killing and expelling civilians, why not send back all of the unit, including Sasa Cvetan, straight away. Third, in its final analysis at paragraph 2155, the Chamber concludes that Djordjevic was aware of the "lack of investigation." But that is inconsistent with its earlier finding at paragraph 1966 where it said that there was a lack of any proper investigation. And even that is plainly wrong. People were investigated and prosecuted, ultimately sentenced to a very lengthy term of imprisonment. Fourthly, what about the finding at paragraph 1948 of the judgement that the redeployed Skorpions committed further crimes in the Jezerce mountain area. It is, we suggest, rather revealing that the Trial Chamber sought to discern Djordjevic's criminal liability on this basis. You will note that no such crimes were alleged in the indictment, they have not been tried, Djordjevic does not stand convicted of them. These allegations remain disputed. No reasonable Trial Chamber would base a conviction on some hint of uncharged and unlitigated events. And it seems clear, if you look at paragraph 1948 of the judgement, that KLA were in the area. Fifthly, the Trial Chamber fails to consider the reality of the circumstances of the redeployment. What if the continued NATO onslaught, the risk of land invasion, made it a difficult but, nevertheless, an understandable decision in all of the circumstances, to send a portion of those forces to try to hold the mountains. Now, if we may conclude by returning to paragraph 2155 of the judgement, there you see that Djordjevic was personally and directly involved in the incorporation of, it is said, a notorious paramilitary unit. It says that after the atrocity they were withdrawn but "no investigation followed." It says that Djordjevic was aware of the "lack of investigation" but nonetheless authorised the redeployment "a few days later." Now, that paragraph, in our respectful submission, is filled of findings that no reasonable Trial Chamber could make. Now, before we leave this topic of Podujevo, why do we say that this raises issues for an appellate court? We have highlighted 15 areas meriting your intervention. Djordjevic faced a largely circumstantial case from which the Trial Chamber inferred his mens rea and attributed this crime and others to him. And our submission on appeal is that other inferences plainly existed. Contrary to the approach the Trial Chamber took, Podujevo in some ways mitigates Djordjevic's guilt. Could Djordjevic have done better? Probably. But is Djordjevic's conduct in the circumstances so bad to have been criminal? Perhaps not as the Trial Chamber suggested. Crucially, is this really the conduct of the most central surviving member of the JCE? In our submission it's not. And also, Podujevo doesn't fit with the Trial Chamber's conclusions on other issues. For example, no reasonable Trial Chamber would fail to weigh the events in Podujevo against its conclusions about Djordjevic concealing dead bodies. Now, as you know, Djordjevic's role concealing crimes together with the Skorpions occupies the majority of the section of the judgement about his role and intent. Now, at trial Djordjevic admitted that he was involved in concealment. His case was in, summary, that he got involved belatedly, reluctantly, to a limited extent, and only once bodies literally started to surface inside Serbia. In effect, he was not in the JCE but panicked when he learned about bodies surfacing. Now, this defence should not have been so readily dismissed. The events at Podujevo are consistent with that defence. For the crime site which the Trial Chamber concluded Djordjevic is most directly implicated, there is no cover-up. This is more than an anomaly. It calls into question the Trial Chamber's assessment of Djordjevic because it's a discrepancy that the Trial Chamber doesn't weigh and it doesn't explain. The Trial Chamber erred repeatedly when it concluded that Djordjevic was the lynch pin of the JCE. You might consider that other modes of liability, other than JCE, better reflect Djordjevic's overall responsibility for events in Kosovo and Podujevo is a good illustration of why. Now, with your permission, we'll now move to the first part of your first question, how the areas of responsibility of Zekovic and Stevanovic impacted Djordjevic's authority as an assistant minister. It might be that your question is motivated by paragraphs 43 and 44 of the judgement. We suggest that those paragraphs are cryptic and contain clear errors meriting your intervention. At paragraph 43 the Trial Chamber found as follows: "... any limitation to Djordjevic's power by reason of the allocation of an area of responsibility to another Assistant Minister would only arise where there is an overlap between the specific responsibility of another Assistant Minister and the general authority of Djordjevic as Chief of the RJB." The Trial Chamber then said "there is no evidence to support the idea that this was the case." But then in paragraph 44, the next paragraph, the Trial Chamber found as follows: "... the Assistant Ministers held high-ranking posts in the MUP and were responsible for their particular fields of authority. It does not accept," the Trial Chamber, that is, "does not accept that this allocation of responsibility had the effect of diminishing Djordjevic's authority as head of the RJB." Now, these findings don't make any sense. First the Trial Chamber says that Djordjevic's power is only reduced if there was an overlap between the specific responsibilities of assistant ministers and his authority as chief of the RJB. Next the Chamber says that assistant ministers were indeed responsible for particular fields of authority but, for reasons that are not explained by the Chamber, somehow this didn't diminish Djordjevic's overall authority. And this is on a crucial issue in this case: Djordjevic's overall role in the MUP. We say this reasoning is inadequate. What the Trial Chamber is doing here is concluding that Djordjevic was the number two man in the MUP, that his powers were only just short of the minister's. And we say that the Trial Chamber was misled by suggestions by a couple of witnesses, Vasiljevic and K87, who said that Djordjevic was the number two man. But these witnesses just couldn't know this. Vasiljevic was in the army and K87 was right at the very bottom of the RJB. The Trial Chamber was misled by misperceptions rather than the altogether less exciting reality. Now, in paragraph 43, the Trial Chamber briefly analysed the relationship between rank in the MUP versus role as an assistant minister. And Djordjevic's case was that these two things, rank versus assistant minister, were separate issues. Just because he held superior rank in the police to Zekovic or Stevanovic or other assistant ministers, that did not mean that he could tell them what to do. Now, in this paragraph, 43, you see the finding that the Chamber was "not convinced" by what it characterised as Djordjevic's assertion about the nature of police ranks within the Ministry of Interior. In fact, Djordjevic's so-called assertion was corroborated by the evidence of Misic, who was the only other assistant minister and who explained that his boss was the minister, not Djordjevic. See transcript pages 14068 to 9, and 14073 to 14076. Now, we would pause here to note that the Prosecution had Stevanovic on their 65 ter list but they didn't call him. Similarly, they said they would call Markovic, another assistant minister, but they didn't call him. So on a crucial issue, a crucial issue, that goes to the heart of Djordjevic's role in the ministry, the Trial Chamber makes contradictory findings, it fails to consider highly relevant evidence, and then it puts the onus on Djordjevic to prove the position when the onus was on the Prosecution to prove that assistant ministers were all subordinate to Djordjevic rather than, as the plain language of their job title suggests, the minister. Instead we then have this cryptic language about potential effect of overlapping responsibilities. So what was the actual position? What is it we say that the Trial Chamber failed to deal with? We have submissions on two areas. Firstly, in case it assists, we will briefly point you to the relevant documents on the areas of responsibility of Zekovic and Stevanovic, indeed the assistant ministers more generally. Secondly, we'll then summarise the findings on Stevanovic and Zekovic and make brief submissions on how their role impacted Djordjevic. The point here is that Djordjevic's authority was more attenuated than the Trial Chamber concluded. And the Trial Chamber only reached its conclusion because it failed to grapple with the issue. And that issue is that the MUP hierarchy was, in reality, a complex web of fiefdoms, tensions, checks and balances, that served the ultimate goal of preserving the minister of the interior's ultimate power. Turning firstly to the relevant laws. We will of course also look at how things worked in practice, but on the laws, rather than try your patience by reading them out, we would propose to identify them and then make two short points on their effect. The first document is the Law on State Administration, and for the transcript that's from April 1992. It's Exhibit P69. See Article 46. The second document we'd refer you to is the Serbian government decree establishing the principles that apply to posts within the ministries. It was published in 1994. It was Exhibit P258. And Article 18(2) of that says that an assistant minister - and this really is crucial - is "directly responsible" to the minister. The third document is a dispatch sent by the minister on the role of assistant ministers from June 1997. It was Exhibit P263. It's a single-page document, and in it you can see the minister setting out Stevanovic's and Zekovic's fields of responsibility. The fourth and penultimate document is the Rules on the Internal Organisation of the Ministry of the Interior and it's from 1997. It was Exhibit P357. And this document sets out the jurisdictions of administrations within the RJB. See in particular Articles 1, 13, 15, 17, 23, and 24. The final document is the minister's decision in December 1998 on the ministerial collegium. It was Exhibit D258 [sic]. And you see in that document that collegium members report directly to the minister, not to Djordjevic. Now, rather than deal with these documents, the Trial Chamber based its conclusions on the MUP hierarchy, on Vasiljevic, and somebody at the very bottom of the RJB. Had it addressed the laws, at least two interesting points emerge. Firstly, one sees an overlap between the jurisdictions, if I can put it like that, of assistant ministers and what is referred to as administrations within the RJB. Precisely the overlap the Trial Chamber alludes to in its cryptic paragraph 43. We see that most clearly when one compares Exhibit P357 with Exhibit P263. Stevanovic and Zekovic's roles as assistant ministers overlaid administrations within the RJB. We also say that Exhibit P263, which is the minister's dispatch, is a significant reduction in the powers of the head of the RJB. It shows that at the same time Djordjevic is appointed as acting head of the RJB in that same document, fiefdoms are created for Zekovic and Stevanovic and others. And importantly, you will see that Exhibit P263 is sent by the minister to nearly everybody in the MUP. So this is an unequivocal statement about the location of power. Yes, Djordjevic is appointed head of the RJB at that time, but at the same time the minister is dispersing power to other assistant ministers. Secondly, one sees that assistant ministers were directly responsible to the minister, not Djordjevic. We've said, as I've mentioned already, you see that in Exhibit P258 [Realtime transcript read in error "P257"], Article 18(2). And similarly, in Exhibit D208, you can see assistant ministers answering directly to the minister, not via Djordjevic, who, after all, was just another assistant minister. Now, combined, we say that these documents suggest that the MUP had something of a split personality. A line of control was created whereby the minister, through his assistant ministers with their zones of responsibility, could control administrations of the RJB. Where there was overlap, Djordjevic's role was diminished. Now, at the same time, administrations within the RJB were subordinate to Djordjevic. Now -- and we do not dispute that people that the assistant minister would control in the RJB would still recognise that Djordjevic was the chief of the RJB. But ultimately, and the relevance of this is that you have a tension that pulls away from Djordjevic. And why? Because it solidifies the reins of power in the hands of the minister of the interior. Now, this isn't just our interpretation of the laws. There was evidence of the practical implications of this set-up. We would mention Exhibit D261 at this stage because the Trial Chamber thought it significant in another context. This is an order sent by Misic, the assistant minister, instructing SUP chiefs about identification documentation. Now, at paragraph 2079 of the judgement, the Trial Chamber suggests that this is an ominous document because it states that SUPs should, it says, "postpone the designation of personal identification numbers until further notice." Even though this was sent to all of the SUPs in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, the Trial Chamber tied this document to instances where Kosovo Albanians had their identification documents confiscated illegally. Now, briefly, if you read the document, you see that it's actually only discussing the suspension of the issuance of new identity numbers because the computer system was affected by the NATO bombing. Now, this would only affect newborn babies getting an identification number for the very first time. It does not mean and it cannot mean that somebody who had their documentation destroyed by a rank-and-file police officer at the border could not get a replacement. They would have the same number as before. But we digress here because the important point for present purposes is that this document is sent by Misic to all of the SUPs. It does not come from, nor is it sent to or copied to, Djordjevic. So this is an assistant minister, Misic, controlling his designated area without Djordjevic. Moving to the practical reality of Stevanovic's and Zekovic's roles, now Djordjevic's defence at trial was that, among other things, Stevanovic came to take the hands-on role on the ground in Kosovo for the minister. You see clear evidence of this in practice, but the Trial Chamber's rejection of it was only possible because it did not deal with the points we've just identified. Now, on the 21st of December, 1998, there was a ministerial staff meeting attended by the minister. Djordjevic was not there. Rather, it was first Lukic, then Stevanovic who chaired the meeting and gave instructions. You see if you look at the minutes, and they're at Exhibit P1043, you see Stevanovic conveying expressly the minister's orders, not Djordjevic's. On the 4th of April, so we're moving into the war now, we have a ministerial staff meeting in Kosovo. And again, Stevanovic is there, Djordjevic is not. The minutes are Exhibit P764. On the 7th of May, Stevanovic attends a ministerial staff meeting and gives detailed instructions to those present on anti-terrorist operations and clearing up the terrain, it said. Djordjevic is not there. That's Exhibit P771, I would refer you to pages 10 and 11 in particular. On the 11th of May, Stevanovic attends another ministerial staff meeting and updates his instructions on anti-terrorist operations, among other things. That's Exhibit P345, pages 7 to 9 in particular. Now, Djordjevic's defence was that power had shifted away from him towards those chosen by the minister and physically present in Kosovo, in particular the ministerial staff for Kosovo which answered to the minister rather than Djordjevic. And we outline in our appeal brief how the Trial Chamber failed to grapple with a key aspect of that decision, Exhibit P57. And the head of the minister's staff, Sreten Lukic, answered, not reported, answered to the minister rather than Djordjevic. No reasonable Trial Chamber would have rejected Djordjevic's defence without grappling with the reality of Stevanovic's role. Turning now to Zekovic. Unlike Stevanovic, the Trial Chamber did not find him to have been a member of the JCE. See paragraph 2122. Indeed, the findings on him are much more limited. But contrary to the repeated suggestion by the Trial Chamber, it's plain that he was not the head of an administration in the RJB. That role for joint affairs was held by Todorovic. See, for example, Exhibit D208, page 4, item 13. One further point of interest is the finding that Zekovic arranged for the collection of bodies from Kosovo, specifically Pristina and Kosovska Mitrovica, and their direct transportation to the Petrovo Selo PJP centre in east Serbia. Now, there was no direct evidence that Djordjevic was involved in this. Indeed, we say that it contrasts with Djordjevic's role at Podujevo, as we have already discussed. Now, why is all this a relevant appellate issue? Well, unlike his predecessors, Djordjevic as chief of the RJB was not the deputy minister of the interior. He was just an assistant minister, like the other assistant ministers. Yes, he was chief of the RJB, but what you plainly see is a marginalisation of that office, particularly in respect of Kosovo for which a ministerial staff is created on the ground. So you see a concentration of power with both the ministerial staff and the Joint Command, which are both in Kosovo, in Pristina. And so Djordjevic remains a sort of figurehead for the RJB, but his role in relation to Kosovo is incrementally reduced. Now, a reasonable Trial Chamber would have grappled with this set-up in the Ministry of Interior. It would not have made these cryptic and confusing findings at paragraphs 43 and 44 of the judgement. Had it properly dealt with this issue, it would have to weigh this reduction in the power of Djordjevic's office. And when you read the judgement as a whole, the obvious difference with Djordjevic's involvement in Kosovo in 1998 compared to the indictment period, the obvious difference. In 1998 he was physically there overseeing about a third, the Trial Chamber found, of police operations that summer. He attended lots of Joint Command meetings and, on occasion, ministerial staff meetings. But in 1999, his role is much more removed. We say this rather raises the question as to whether Djordjevic really made a significant contribution to the JCE in 1999. Alternatively, even if you conclude that Djordjevic remained in the JCE, this reduced role merits a significant reduction in sentence. For that reason, the resolution of this -- of the role of assistant ministers is of vital importance to Djordjevic's appeal. I'm told that the transcript page 23, line 4, refers to D258. Exhibit D258 should be 208. And then at page 24, at line 13, it says P257, that should be P258.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOPKINS
utterances.text: Now, turning then, if I may, to question two posed by the Appeals Chamber, which we were asked to discuss in relation to Djordjevic's 11th ground of appeal, the implications of the fact that the Trial Chamber didn't make explicit findings on substantial contribution in relation to forcible transfer and did not make explicit findings in relation to specific direction. Now, when the Trial Chamber additionally convicted Djordjevic of aiding and abetting, it failed to make the necessary findings and it failed to give an adequately reasoned judgement. Its approach, we say, elides aiding and abetting with JCE. A careful and reasonable Trial Chamber would not have done this. We suggest that it is this erroneous elision of aiding and abetting in JCE that gives rise to your second question. Before making submissions on specific direction, I will address that part of your question about the fact that the Trial Chamber did not make explicit findings on substantial contribution to forcible transfer. This question is presumably generated by paragraph 2163 of the judgement, where the Trial Chamber concluded that Djordjevic's acts had a substantial effect on the perpetration by MUP forces of the crimes of murder, deportation, and persecutions in Kosovo. So forcible transfer is noticeable by its absence in that paragraph. But then in the very next paragraph, 2164, the Trial Chamber concluded that Djordjevic did indeed aid and abet forcible transfer, and then similarly in the disposition, that the Trial Chamber concludes that Djordjevic aided and abetted forcible transfer. So there is, therefore an inconsistency in the Trial Chamber's treatment. It is doubly odd that Djordjevic was found to have made a substantial contribution to persecutions and convicted of persecutions by means of forcible transfer without an explicit finding that he made a substantial contribution to the underlying crime of forcible transfer. Now, frankly, we are at a loss to explain paragraph 2163 of the judgement. It could be a simple mistake, some missed wording, or there might be some unexplained logic to it. We just don't know. But be that as it may, we must address the question of whether a finding of substantial contribution to forcible transfer is nevertheless implicit in the Trial Chamber's findings. And on this, an important point, we say, arises from paragraph 2163 and it's this: The finding of substantial effect, as it's described there, is in relation to MUP crimes only, so not the VJ and not other forces. Now, why does that matter? Well, this is a more limited finding than a substantial contribution to all crimes in Kosovo. And it seems to be a deliberate finding because it's expressly repeated at paragraph 2194. Now, this approach of limiting Djordjevic's aiding and abetting liability to crimes by MUP forces is consistent with the approach in Milutinovic where Ojdanic and Lazarevic were convicted of aiding and abetting VJ crimes in their case but not other forces like the MUP. And the Office of the Prosecutor did not appeal that approach. Returning to Djordjevic's case, despite this limited finding of Djordjevic's contribution to MUP crimes, in the disposition and sentence you see that Djordjevic is, for reasons unexplained, convicted of aiding and abetting all of the crimes in Kosovo irrespective of the perpetrators, be they MUP, VJ, or anybody else. Now, this is yet another example of metamorphosis in the Trial Chamber's findings. It suggests to us that the Trial Chamber's decision to additionally convict Djordjevic of aiding and abetting was something of an afterthought. It does not seem to have been rigorously thought through by the Trial Chamber, which may be why you see a failure to make explicit findings and are then faced with the difficulties when you're considering whether the necessary findings are actually implicit in the Trial Chamber's approach. Now, we will address you on the appropriate remedy after discussing the lack of explicit findings on specific direction. So turning then to specific direction. We say that Djordjevic actually lost out from the paucity of the Trial Chamber's reasoning on aiding and abetting. If one looks at Djordjevic's conduct through a specific direction lens, as the Appeals Chamber in Perisic recently confirmed that the Trial Chamber should, we suggest that a picture comes into focus that his relationship to crimes in Kosovo was more remote and attenuated than the Trial Chamber concluded. Now, the relevant paragraphs of the judgement are 2163 and 2194. 2163 is the finding on Djordjevic's actus reus for aiding and abetting. 2194 is a further justification, and it suggests that a key issue for the Trial Chamber's conclusion here was Djordjevic's role in the concealment of crimes. But dealing firstly with other aspects of Djordjevic's actus reus, such as his overall role in the MUP and his involvement sending the Skorpions to Kosovo, we would make the short point that the circumstances faced by the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in 1999, such actions were not necessarily specifically directed to crimes. Now, you might suspect that they were, but we would respectfully suggest that it is reasonably possible that they were not. Now, Perisic says that in most cases where an accused is remote from the location of crimes, the provision of general assistance which could be used for both lawful and unlawful activities will not be sufficient alone to prove that such aid was specifically directed to crimes. And we suggest that much of Djordjevic's conduct in all of the circumstances could have been general assistance for lawful activities. Indeed, the immediate removal of the Skorpions after Podujevo rather suggests that his conduct was not directed towards such crimes. Like the Perisic case, Djordjevic was primarily based in Belgrade, whereas crimes took place hundreds of kilometres away. And we say that Djordjevic's intermittent visits to Kosovo in 1999 do not change that approach. He was physically remote from the crimes. Now, having said all that, as I mentioned, a key point for the Trial Chamber was Djordjevic's role in the concealment of crimes. And on that issue, at first sight, the Perisic judgement does not seem to assist Djordjevic greatly. You would likely conclude that concealing crimes is not general assistance for otherwise lawful activities. Now, we should also acknowledge that Judge Agius and Judge Meron in Perisic considered that mens rea is relevant when assessing whether acts are specifically directed towards crimes. And in this case we are faced, for now anyway, with the finding that Djordjevic was a member of the JCE. So although the Trial Chamber failed to make explicit findings about specific direction, and although the criteria of specific direction, we say, sheds a different light on some of Djordjevic's actions, because of these concealment operations, Perisic does not seem, at first sight anyway, to be decisive in Djordjevic's favour. But the question then becomes whether Djordjevic's involvement in the concealment of crimes is an implicit finding that his acts and omissions were specifically directed towards crimes. Now, an instinctive answer to that question might be, of course, such acts were specifically directed to the crime. But we would respectfully suggest that such an instinctive answer would be wrong in law. In our submission, assisting in reburials like Djordjevic did does not necessarily entail criminal liability for the earlier crime. The law, we say, requires a prior agreement between the perpetrator and the aider and abettor. Now, I will develop that submission in a moment, but before doing so we must overcome a factual finding that Djordjevic was party to a sort of prior agreement with Milosevic and the minister Stojiljkovic, because if that factual finding remains undisturbed, our submission on the law faces a hurdle. Now, the Trial Chamber found that a plan existed to conceal the bodies of Kosovo Albanians killed during the indictment period. You see that at paragraph 1967. It found that there was a co-ordinated operation to clear Kosovo of evidence of crimes and that the operation was conducted under Djordjevic's direction after an order by the minister and President Milosevic. You see that in paragraph 1980. Now, this is a startling finding. At paragraph 2112 and 2117, there is another startling finding that Djordjevic attended a meeting in March 1999 in Milosevic's office with Stojiljkovic and Markovic and that he was later delegated this cover-up operation by the minister. Now, we invite the Appeals Chamber here to draw a clear line as to what is and what is not acceptable reasoning by a fact-finder. The Chamber conceded that the evidence of these supposed meetings was not, in the Trial Chamber's words, first hand. Now, we recognise, of course, that a Trial Chamber can rely on hearsay evidence, but with great respect to the Trial Chamber, that rather understates its approach to this issue. The only evidence of these meetings was the first report by the Working Group set up in May 2001. It is Exhibit P387, and it is summarised at paragraphs 1373 and 2112 of the judgement. Now, the information giving rise to the Working Group's suggestion that these meetings happened was a supposed statement by the former chief of the RDB, Radomir Markovic, that he is said to have given while he was in prison. First point, even if such a statement was made by Markovic, a reasonable Trial Chamber would have to weigh its reliability given the source and the circumstances in which it was given. And you don't see that in this judgement. Second point, Markovic's statement was not in evidence in this case. Indeed, the Working Group did not claim to have seen it. Instead, it is said that notes were taken of it by a member of the Working Group, notes of Markovic's statement. Third point, those notes that were supposedly taken of Markovic's statement, they weren't in evidence either. So the basis for the Trial Chamber's findings was the evidence that somebody had seen a note that somebody had taken of a purported statement. And we should also note again that the Prosecution had Markovic on their 65 ter list but didn't call him. Now, even leaving aside the Defence's case at trial that the Working Group was a hatchet job looking to blame Djordjevic, there is hearsay and then there is this. Now, of course the Trial Chamber, all Trial Chambers, have a wide discretion in the assessment of evidence, but that discretion is not unlimited, and in our respectful submission, this is as clear an example as you can get of a Trial Chamber overreaching. Not even the Prosecution in their closing brief attempted to suggest that these meetings took place. Now, the obvious point to make against us here is that, well, a concealment operation did take place, so it was not unreasonable to conclude that there was a meeting at which it was planned. Well, we still say that you cannot reverse engineer Djordjevic's involvement in such a meeting in that way. Indeed, the fact that there was no cover-up at Podujevo, the crime to which Djordjevic -- the Trial Chamber thought Djordjevic was most closely related, rather suggests he was not party to such an agreement. So we say that a reasonable inference remained that Djordjevic's role was far more attenuated than the Trial Chamber concluded. Now, the bodies that were found in the river Danube near Tekija in eastern Serbia were moved in two truckloads to the Batajnica SAJ centre and buried there on or around the 8th of April, 1999. There followed further truckloads of bodies arriving at Batajnica that Djordjevic was involved with. But the extent of this evidence, we suggest, is that Djordjevic's role was limited to Serbia proper, when he learned that bodies surfaced there. No reasonable Trial Chamber would draw the conclusory inference that Djordjevic knew about or was involved with any original crimes or burials in Kosovo, subsequent disinterment, and then secret transportation to Serbia. Indeed, the lack of such an operation in Podujevo is revealing of this. So Djordjevic's acts were not specifically directed to crimes against Kosovo Albanians; had they been, one would surely see a cover-up in Podujevo. On Batajnica, the timing of Djordjevic's actions and knowledge is relevant. We suggest that here again the Trial Chamber's findings changed during the course of the judgement. For example, at paragraph 1347, the Chamber concluded that Djordjevic knew that the trucks were headed from Tekija to Batajnica. But at paragraph 1356, this becomes that Djordjevic ordered the trucks to go from Tekija to Batajnica. So there is a clear difference. Similarly, there is an issue as to whether Djordjevic was involved in sending further trucks to Batajnica or whether he was merely informed that trucks had arrived there and he then arranged reburials. On this, at paragraph 1337 of the judgement, the Chamber concludes there that Djordjevic told K87 in advance about each arrival. But if you look to the evidence, you see that nowhere is it suggested that Djordjevic actually knew in advance that trucks were going to arrive rather than merely having himself found out the trucks arrived there and then taking steps to arrange reburials. The significance of all this, we say, is that Djordjevic was more removed from the cover-up than the Trial Chamber concluded. Yes, he became involved in it and, yes, his conduct merits criticism. But the highest at which the evidence could be put is of an ill-judged, somewhat panicked afterthought. Now, if we may turn briefly to the law on specific direction in the context of omissions and cover-ups. The Popovic trial judgement, in particular at paragraph 1032 and 1083, held that reburial operations are not crimes in and of themselves under the Statute. An accused is not held criminally responsible for the reburials; rather, any involvement in a reburial operation is evidence, relevant evidence, to be weighed to decide whether an accused is criminally responsible for the earlier deaths of those individuals. Now, we make a similar point in paragraphs 239 to 243 of our brief. The approach in Popovic isn't new. It's consistent with the Blagojevic trial judgement, paragraphs 731 and 745. And in Blagojevic, the Trial Chamber found that a reburial operation that occurred after scrutiny of events in Srebrenica had not been agreed upon at the time of the killings there. The Trial Chamber held that a prior agreement must exist between the principal and the person who subsequently aids and abets; paragraph 731 of that judgement. So the Trial Chamber in Blagojevic required a prior agreement between the aider and abettor and the principal in order for acts performed after the underlying crime to constitute aiding and abetting. Similarly in Aleksovski, the Trial Chamber held that aiding and abetting may occur after the crime. But the Trial Chamber stressed that this must have been promised beforehand -- promised to the perpetrator beforehand that the aider and abettor would perform certain acts after the crime had been committed. You see that in the Aleksovski judgement paragraph 62. And we also rely on the Strugar trial judgement decided less than two weeks after Blagojevic. And in Strugar, the Prosecution alleged that the accused had not punished his troops for shelling the Old Town of Dubrovnik and that this amounted to aiding and abetting unlawful shelling. The Trial Chamber was not satisfied that conduct like this after the offences were committed could have had a direct and substantial effect on the commission of the earlier offences. It thus declined to convict Strugar of aiding and abetting and he was instead convicted under Article 7(3). Now, obviously the approach in those cases doesn't bind you, but we would suggest it's interesting that three different trial judgements involving nine different Judges have recognised that particular criteria are applied to assistance given after a crime is committed. And we say that with a reburial operation or cover-up, an explicit demonstration is needed that those acts directly affected the earlier crime. In some cases, this is said to require a showing of a prior agreement between the accused and the principal, such that the principal would commit the crime, safe in the knowledge that their crime would be covered up. So our submission is here that when one looks to apply Perisic to concealment operations or a failure to punish, one still needs to identify how that concealment encouraged the perpetrators to commit crimes. As opposed, for example, to simply helping the perpetrator avoid justice. More often than not what you will need to see is an agreement between the aider and abettor and the perpetrator. Now, the Trial Chamber, in conclusion, should have weighed the suggestion that Djordjevic attended ominous meetings with the obviously contradictory sequence of events in Podujevo. In our submission, the inference of any agreement or secret master plan should never have been drawn. Instead, the reasonable inference remains that Djordjevic's conduct in all of this was not specifically directed to crimes; rather, he was drawn into an ill-conceived cover-up after the fact. But what about the Prosecution's argument that they make in their response brief that Djordjevic's conduct was not after the fact, it was not so much a failure to punish because, they say, and they point out correctly, there was a series of cover-ups from 8th off April onwards. Well, we can see some force in their argument, but it becomes very, very difficult to apply it to the facts of this case. Firstly, you could not convict Djordjevic on that basis of crimes committed before the 8th of April; and secondly, you would, we suggest, need to identify which crimes Djordjevic actually assisted and in which location. Now, we argue in our appeal brief that this section of the trial judgement on aiding and abetting is so inadequately reasoned that the fairest approach is to quash all of Djordjevic's aiding and abetting convictions. And we say that because if there were careful findings on aiding and abetting, we would have been able to challenge them on appeal. We would challenge, for example, and this is just an example, any suggestion that concealing bodies from one location means that a person somehow aids and abets, for example, wanton destruction in another location on a different day. So the debate here, we respectfully suggest, is that Djordjevic's conduct is perhaps more coherently expressed in the context of Article 7(3) rather than contorting Article 7(1), especially when it is clear that the Trial Chamber has not applied relevant criteria. Now, that concludes my submissions on the second question. My submissions on the third and fourth questions are much briefer. I don't know whether now is a convenient moment or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I think it is. And we have recovered the lost time, so we will still reconvene at 11.00, and you will then proceed with your submissions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOPKINS
utterances.text: Turning then to the third question posed by the Appeals Chamber, which is to discuss in relation to Djordjevic's 13th ground of appeal and with a reference to the trial record whether for the purpose of establishing the crime of deportation and in light of customary international law, a de facto border existed between Kosovo and Montenegro. Now, as I say, my submissions on this third question and also the fourth question are much briefer than what's been before. Now, our submission on this third question is straightforward. Properly understood, deportation is the compelled movement of a person from the territory in one party's control to the territory in another party's control. Usually that will be across international state boundaries, and that is the default position subject to limited exceptions, none of which are relevant to this case. We suggest that definition is clear, it's easily understood, it is consistent with the common understanding of what it means to deport somebody. For example, Black's Law Dictionary defines deportation as the "act or an instance of removing a person to another country ... the expulsion or transfer of an alien from a country." This contrasts with the crime of forcible transfer as an inhumane act which is forced movement of people within a country. Now, you have asked whether a de facto border existed between Kosovo and Montenegro in the indictment period. Now, our submission is that the border between Kosovo and Montenegro was a de jure internal administrative boundary within the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. All it did was separate the province of Kosovo from the Republic of Montenegro. So those who left Kosovo for Montenegro may have been forcibly transferred, but they were not deported. They remained at all times within the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Now, firstly on the light cast by customary international law to this question, there is, of course, a discussion of this in, among other places, the Stakic appeals judgement paragraphs 290 to 303, and Judge Shahabuddeen's dissent in the same case, and also Judge Schomburg's dissent in the Naletilic case. Now, we will not rehearse those analyses but we would draw out a few points. The Stakic judgement noted that many of the international materials while expressly prohibiting deportation don't define it. Importantly, the Stakic judgement recognised at paragraph 300 what it described --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry, you are referring to the Stakic trial judgement or the appeal judgement?

utterances.speaker: MR. HOPKINS
utterances.text: Sorry. Excuse me, the appeal judgement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Just for clarity. I knew you were, but for the record it's better to have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOPKINS
utterances.text: So the Stakic appeal judgement paragraph 300 describes the default position that deportation requires expulsion across a de jure border, and then we say this is the key point, to another country. So the Appeals Chamber in Stakic recognised the need for a border to be crossed for the crime of deportation to be established and said it's a border with another country. It then said that the question of whether a de facto border is sufficient for the purposes of the crime of deportation should be examined on a case-by-case basis. The Appeals Chamber in Stakic quashed a conviction for deportation across constantly changing front lines on the basis that that had given a greater scope to the crime of deportation than existed in customary international law. Now, Judge Shahabuddeen dissented from this border requirement, but we would dwell briefly on his analysis because it is instructive. The issue in Stakic was whether or not forced movement across a changing front line was deportation, and then reversing the Trial Chamber, the Appeals Chamber held that it was not. Now, Judge Shahabuddeen's dissent is premised on his understanding that the essence of deportation is forced movement from the control of one party to the control of another. See paragraph 69 of his dissent, where he says: "When one speaks of deportation across a border, what is involved is 'forced displacement' of civilians; but that also happens," he says, "in the case of forced displacement of civilians across a front line separating an area of a state," and this is the key point, "under the control of one party from an area of the same state to under the control of an opposing party." He distinguishes forcible transfer because what the wrong-doer is doing in the case of deportation is, in Judge Shahabuddeen's words, "getting rid" of people. Now, this is significant because when Kosovo Albanians crossed the border to Montenegro, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia did not get rid of them, if I can put it crudely. They remained within the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Now, Judge Schomburg in Naletilic argued against any cross-border requirement, but his dissent is strictly obiter. We should, though, draw your attention to the fact that Judge Schomburg rightly notes that the Nuremberg judgement does not focus on the destination of people who were forcibly moved before convicting Nazi leaders of deportation. We should also point out that many of the subsequent Nuremberg trials appear to reject a cross-border element. And you can find those cases well summarised in pages 218 to 220 of the recent book by Kevin Jon Heller about the subsequent Nuremberg trials. But, in our respectful submission, when one looks at those cases one is not really seeing deportation applied as a term of art. The accused in those cases could just as easily have been convicted of forcible transfer, and it is, we would suggest, dangerous to place too much reliance on those cases for the precise meaning of the word "deportation." So our submission is that properly understood and consistent with customary international law, deportation is the expulsion beyond the control of one belligerent into the control of another. In our case, the Trial Chamber's conclusion that the border between Kosovo and Montenegro was a de facto border is at paragraph 1683 of the judgement. The Trial Chamber relied on Kosovo's previous autonomy, Montenegro's status as a republic, and the armed conflict in Kosovo, and also the effect of the displacement on the individuals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One question, why does it have to be another belligerent? In other words, why do you confine it to deportation from the control of one belligerent into the control of another? Couldn't the deportation be to an area, to a country, or across a border to somewhere --

utterances.speaker: MR. HOPKINS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- which is not involved in the conflict at all?

utterances.speaker: MR. HOPKINS
utterances.text: Yes, I would accept that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOPKINS
utterances.text: But in accepting that, the person is still transferred to somewhere -- a jurisdiction that is in control of another party, another country, albeit not a belligerent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KHAN
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Judge Khan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KHAN
utterances.text: When you say "party," what do you mean by "party"?

utterances.speaker: MR. HOPKINS
utterances.text: I mean another a country, another international country.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KHAN
utterances.text: Another country, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOPKINS
utterances.text: And I say that is consistent with the common understanding of the meaning "deportation." So we would respectfully suggest that the Trial Chamber failed to apply an essential element of deportation which, as we say, is the expulsion of a person into the control of another party, in another country. That criteria was not satisfied when people were transferred from Kosovo to Montenegro. We struggle to see how crossing the border from Kosovo to Montenegro is any different from crossing municipality boundaries within Kosovo. The quality of any de facto border that is most relevant, we say, involves crossing to another party. And that just didn't happen when Kosovo Albanians went to Montenegro. Now, in 2013, today, the answer would be different, but in 1999 the answer is clear. To start calling it a de facto border seems to us to be artificial. It is a stretch and in our respectful submission introduces needless uncertainty into the law to start calling what is a de jure internal administrative boundary within a country a de facto border.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So you say both Kosovo and Montenegro were under the control of the same party?

utterances.speaker: MR. HOPKINS
utterances.text: Both under the control of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOPKINS
utterances.text: In 1999. The position is, of course, different today. Moving then to our submissions on your fourth question, we are asked to discuss in relation to Djordjevic's 16th ground of appeal, whether the indictment charged certain events. And our answer in relation to each of your questions posed is no. The indictment did not charge any of these incidents, and if we may begin by briefly looking at each in turn. The first is deportation from Kladernica between the 12th and the 15th of April, 1999, and the relevant paragraph is 72(c) of the indictment where Kladernica is mentioned as being the subject of an attack beginning on or around the 25th of March, so some three weeks earlier. Now, you will note that Djordjevic was convicted of forcible transfer for that attack - you see that in paragraphs 1702 to 1704, and 1630 to 1631 - but the later different attack on that village is just not in the indictment. Next, deportation from Suva Reka town between the 7th and the 21st of May. The relevant paragraph there is 72(d) of the indictment, which refers to events in Suva Reka on the 25th and 26th of March for which Djordjevic has been separately convicted. Now, there is no mention in the indictment of these later events in May, and indeed if you look at paragraph 72(d)(i), you will see that it narrows the time-period for Suva Reka to a backstop date of the 1st of April. Next, forcible transfer from the villages of Brocna and Tusilje between the 25th and 26th of March and the 29th of March respectively. The relevant paragraph of the indictment is 72(c) where six villages are mentioned. Brocna and Tusilje are not there. Next, forcible transfer from the village of Cuska on the 14th of May. The relevant paragraph of the indictment is 72(e), where you see that the allegation is limited to the city of Pec on the 27th and the 28th of May. Next, murder in Mala Krusa on the 25th of March. The relevant paragraph of the indictment is again, I think, paragraph 75(c), where one sees references to an unoccupied house and 105 victims are identified in Schedule C to the indictment. As you know, that incident is the Batusa barn killings, but Djordjevic was additionally convicted of persons burnt to death on another house on a different day. And that incident is not in the indictment. Finally, murder in Podujevo on 28th of March, this is the Skorpions that we've already discussed today. The relevant paragraph is 74(l), where one does see the allegation that women and children were killed in the courtyard, as we've discussed, but Djordjevic was additionally convicted of the murder of two men in a nearby cafe and that further incident is not in the indictment. Persecutions, this is the final point, sorry, persecutions through murder of the murder of over 100 people in Pusto Selo on the 31st of March, 1999. You can see that persecutions are identified in paragraph 77(c) of the indictment which refers back to paragraphs 27 and 28 of the indictment and paragraph 75. And killings in Orahovac municipality are identified in paragraphs 75(b) and (c) on the 25th of March, 1999. So there is no mention at all of Pusto Selo or anything remotely like this killing. So we have briefly summarised how those incidents, we say, are not in the indictment. Now, we have brief submissions on the importance of this issue. We say that the form of the indictment in this case and the context in which it was put together are of some significance. Firstly with the form, we say that this was not a vague indictment capable of being cured. It was a very specific indictment. It quite properly identifies specific locations and dates, and by doing so so carefully and explicitly, an accused should be able to rely on it. Turning to the context when the operative indictment in this case was finalised, it was the fourth amended indictment. It was approved in July 2008, and it is essentially the same indictment as that which the accused in the Milutinovic trial faced with a few amendments, including the Podujevo incident. The Prosecution's pre-trial brief was filed on the 1st of September, 2008, and Djordjevic's trial began in January of 2009. Now, the relevant context that we rely on is that the Office of the Prosecutor filed its closing brief in Milutinovic on the 15th of July, 2008, about a week after it finalised the fourth amended indictment in Djordjevic's case. And we say this is relevant because the Office of the Prosecutor must have known exactly what allegations it wanted to charge Djordjevic with, and those allegations are in the fourth amended indictment, nowhere else. So we do not understand why if the Prosecution wanted to charge Djordjevic and hold him criminally responsible for additional crimes, it couldn't put them in the fourth amended indictment. It is also puzzling to us that in our case at paragraph 321 of the Prosecution's response brief to our appeal, the Prosecution states confidently, for example, that deportation from Tusilje on the 29th of March, 1999, was covered by the indictment. It suggests there that all the Trial Chamber did in its judgement was make more detailed findings. But in the Sainovic appeal hearing, the Prosecutor agreed that Tusilje should have been pled in that indictment and that no corrective actions were taken in the pre-trial brief or 65 ter filings. You can see that in the transcript from that hearing on Monday, the 11th of March, 2013, at page 240. So the Prosecution did not amend the fourth amended indictment against Djordjevic to encapsulate these additional allegations about which you've asked. That must have been, we say, a deliberate choice. It had all the witness statements, had all the information it needed. They had just finished the Milutinovic trial about the same events. And we ask the Appeals Chamber to affirm the importance of the indictment. This Tribunal should not, we say, allow the Prosecution to file an indictment after careful consideration and a deliberate choice and then enter additional convictions. Even if some of these crimes are mentioned somewhere in witness statements or a Prosecution witness summary or a brief somewhere, in this case we say it makes no difference because of the context. Now, that concludes my submissions on question four. Unless there are any questions from the Panel, I would now pass over to Ms. O'Leary who will address you on question five.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There are none, so Ms. O'Leary.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm Marie O'Leary and I thank you for the opportunity to address you. I'll be discussing the Djordjevic appeal brief, grounds 18 and 19, with particular focus on the Panel's inquiry regarding concurrent convictions. In its fifth interrogatory, the honourable Chamber has asked the parties to discuss, in relation to our ground of appeal and with reference to the Trial Chamber's findings, why convictions for the crimes on the basis of both commission through participation in a joint criminal enterprise and aiding and abetting based on the same conduct better reflect the totality of Djordjevic's conduct? The short answer, Your Honours, is they don't. No one, not the Trial Chamber in their judgement and not the Prosecution in their response, no one has been able to point to where there is an additional factor considered in one conviction that is not considered in the other that would call for both to better reflect his conduct. In fact, we would submit that it does quite the opposite. As you've read in our brief, the Defence submits that these concurrent convictions are an error of law, one for which we are seeking relief from the Appeals Chamber. And at the outset, all of our Defence submissions on concurrent convictions must be taken with two considerations in mind. The first consideration is that it is unequivocal that Vlastimir Djordjevic was convicted twice for the same conduct. Aside from the clear language that was used in the disposition at paragraphs 2230 and 2231, they clearly list two modes of liability for each count. It's also evident in the Trial Chamber's statement at paragraph 2214. There, in stating that it would "determine sentence accordingly," it considered a JCE 1 liability with an aggravating factor based on superior responsibility. But it also considered that, and I quote, "the accused's conduct was such as to also render him liable to conviction and punishment for aiding and abetting the offences established." It is this language that distinguishes this case from the recent case of Gatete where the Appeals Chamber determined that a mere reference to other modes of liability were not additional convictions. And that's Gatete appeals judgement paragraph 235. There is no question that Mr. Djordjevic was, in fact, convicted on two modes of liability for each of the five counts, and it is unambiguous that the single sentence issued by the Trial Chamber reflected these dual convictions. The second overarching consideration that you must take into mind on our concurrent conviction challenges is that the Defence does not challenge that it can be possible to have multiple convictions under Article 7(1) of the ICTY Statute. And I raise this because the Prosecution has suggested that this was an issue on appeal at paragraphs 373 and 377 of their response. This is not the case.
