Our position is that these specific modes of liability of JCE and aiding and abetting are not permissible concurrent convictions when based on the same conduct. And, Your Honours, in our written submissions both parties have pointed to the fact that concurrent convictions for JCE 1 and aiding and abetting have not been before this Appeals Chamber and we must consider why this specific situation has not arisen. Why, as far as we can ascertain, has Vlastimir Djordjevic been the first person convicted on these two specific modes of liability --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. O'Leary, I haven't heard as yet complaints or remarks from the interpreters, but in my opinion, you are going a little bit too fast, almost also too fast for me. Yes, I am seeing the interpreters --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- nodding, so if you could slow down a little bit --

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Absolutely. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- I would appreciate it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: My apologies. As discussed at length in our brief and reply, the cases relied on by the Trial Chamber for the dual convictions to better reflect conduct - and those are Nahimana, Ndindabahizi, and Kamuhanda - are not instructive. Your Honours, they are not JCE cases. And if we dig deeper to see where these cases found a basis for concurrent convictions under 7(1), we come to the Akayesu trial judgement where at paragraph 468 it states that concurrent convictions are permissible on the same set of facts in three specific circumstances, the third being where it is necessary, and I quote, "to record a conviction for both offences in order to fully describe what the accused did." It goes on to state in that paragraph, 468, "however, the Chamber finds that it is not justifiable to convict an accused of two offences in relation to the same set of facts where ... one offence charges accomplice liability and the other offence charges liability as a principal." The very Chamber that iterated the allowance for concurrent convictions on the same facts to better reflect the totality of an accused's conduct prohibits concurrent convictions for principal liability, JCE, and accomplice liability, aiding and abetting. Once a finding of commission by participation in a JCE is properly made, all other alternatively charged modes of liability fall away. They are subsumed. This is seen in trial judgements and even those that have been issued since briefing. The Trial Chambers at the ICTY have yet adopted the practice of declining to convict on other potential modes of liability after reaching a JCE finding. And this was seen most recently in the Stanisic and Zupljanin trial judgement at volume II, paragraphs 529 and 780; in the Gotovina trial judgement at paragraphs 2375 and 2587; and in the Tolimir trial judgement at paragraph 1174. In stating that it would not make further convictions on modes of liability after reaching a JCE conviction as best encapsulating conduct, the Tolimir Trial Chamber specifically referred to that Milutinovic et al. jurisprudence that we have cited to in our brief. And that's at footnote 4509 of the Tolimir trial judgement. With JCE and aiding and abetting, it comes down to the fundamentals of these modes of liability, one is principal liability and one is accomplice liability, and the principal cannot be the accomplice on the same crimes, just as the accomplice cannot be the principal. And this, we would submit, is common sense. So why is this the first time that the Appeals Chamber has heard of this issue of concurrent convictions for JCE I and aiding and abetting? Because the Trial Chambers know that it is legal error to convict on both and it is a legal error we are asking this honourable Chamber to remedy. So to get to the heart of your question number five, Your Honours, in this case, concurrent convictions do not better reflect the totality of Djordjevic's conduct. Maintaining all of our other grounds of appeal that we have put forward, the Trial Chamber did not give a reasoned opinion as to how such double conviction would better reflect the total of his conduct. Importantly, if we're looking at the specific conduct they analysed, there is not one additional fact that is considered for that aiding and abetting conviction. Paragraph 2163 states that, and I quote: "The accused acted to assist the commission of these crimes," but then it goes on to recall its, I quote, "earlier findings" on conduct, those that were the basis of JCE liability, and in particular we're talking about a lack of investigation and concealment of crimes. The conduct cited as actus reus of the aiding and abetting paragraph at 2163 and 2194 is identical to the conduct established as the actus reus of a significant contribution to a JCE at paragraphs 2155 to 2157. The Gotovina --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down for the sake of the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: My apologies. The Gotovina appeal judgement at paragraph 149 recently noted that "a finding of a significant contribution is not equivalent to a substantial contribution required to enter a conviction for aiding and abetting." In the Djordjevic trial judgement, there is absolutely no explanation as to how that finding, that Djordjevic contributed significantly to a JCE, and that's at paragraph 2158, somehow transforms into one of substantial effect at paragraph 2163 or how he substantially assisted, which are the words used as paragraph 2194. That said, the point where concurrent convictions truly fail to better reflect conduct is in establishing the mens rea. At paragraph 2158, Your Honours, the Trial Chamber made a finding of a JCE I mens rea and it was based on loose circumstantial finding that Djordjevic's crimes, found largely as a failure to investigate and concealment of crimes, were committed with the knowledge of, and I quote, "crimes committed by Serbian forces in Kosovo." Now leaving aside that the nature of such concealment and lack of investigation necessarily includes the knowledge of crimes, knowledge does not point to an actual intention to be a part of a JCE and it doesn't point to a commonality working with persons with a shared common purpose. Much less does it show the specific persecutorial intent necessary for the crime of persecution. And, Your Honours, while intent can be derived circumstantially from knowledge and acts, it must be done beyond a reasonable doubt. It must be the only reasonable conclusion. However, Your Honours, there is reasonable doubt in the Trial Chamber's own analysis. In that exact same paragraph, 2158, the Trial Chamber states that had it not been able to be satisfied with a JCE I finding, it would have been satisfied with a JCE III intent of awareness of the crimes and a willing risk. Paragraph 2158 is extremely telling. It says that the Chamber determined its findings could support a mens rea of either JCE I or JCE III. And by paragraph 2163 we have a third reasonable conclusion of a finding of mens rea, that his knowledge equated to an accomplice liability level, that he knew that his acts were assisting in the commission of crimes. Your Honours, we would submit that there are three distinct levels of mens rea found here: One, intention; two, recklessness; and three, awareness. This, Your Honours, does not provide a reasonable opinion that establishes beyond a reasonable doubt the mental elements necessary to any of these modes of liability. As set out in grounds 10 and 11 of our brief, the Trial Chamber failed to make sufficient findings on the mens rea required for either JCE or aiding and abetting. And to answer this question, it doesn't better reflect the totality of Djordjevic's conduct, it does quite the opposite. We're left wondering what intent was actually found beyond a reasonable doubt. The problem in these concurrent convictions, Your Honours, is not with the nuances of significant contribution versus substantial effect, it is not in the actus reus. It is with the lack of concrete findings of a mens rea for either of these convictions, and if you remove the need to define that mental element beyond a reasonable doubt for conviction, you've erased the element of mens rea in the criminal law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I saw you looking at the clock. You have roughly six minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: This error matters in three ways: One, it is incorrect law generally that must not be allowed to perpetuate as jurisprudence. It is not what was envisioned in the jurisprudence of better reflecting the totality of conduct. Two, it is incorrect law in this case that must be remedied. This is not a theoretical challenge. This is a case against Vlastimir Djordjevic, and multiple convictions create extraneous prejudice. This was cited by the Krstic appeals judgement at paragraph 217 and developed further in the Kunarac appeals judgement at paragraph 169. The third consequence it created is it created an incorrect sentence, and I will come more to that in sentencing briefly. I want to make one point on ground 18(B), Your Honours, with regard to the cumulative convictions that we are challenging. We're saying that the crimes charged as stand-alone crimes of murder, deportation, and forcible transfer in addition to the persecutory crimes, Counts 1, 2, and 3 of the trial judgement are cumulative to Count 5. And so it's with note that I comment on the most recent judgement of the ICTY, in the Stanisic and Zupljanin Trial Chamber that found exactly this: Deportation, forcible transfer, and murder as a crime against humanity are impermissibly cumulative when found as underlying acts of persecution. In refusing to enter separate convictions for the stand-alone counts, the Stanisic and Zupljanin Trial Chamber said to do so would lead to the result of convicting an accused twice for the same crimes. And that's in volume II at paragraph 912. Your Honours, this Appeals Chamber has stated that there is an insoluble nexus between conviction and sentence. And that's the Miodrag Jokic sentencing appeal judgement, paragraph 26. In the present case the conduct has been convicted and punished twice. That's from paragraph 2214 of the trial judgement. And, Your Honours, significantly, we're asking you at a minimum to remove three counts and one mode of liability as based on the same facts and thus impermissibly concurrent and cumulative convictions. They were factored into the consideration of a single sentence and served to raise his sentence. We have outlined further errors in ground 19 of our brief and we're asking you to look at the totality of Mr. Djordjevic's conduct, especially in light of our other grounds of appeal, and quash both convictions of joint criminal enterprise and aiding and abetting as not properly found. These are errors of law that have invalidated the judgement. And subject to any questions, Your Honours, these are my remarks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Then I will pass the floor on briefly for a conclusion by counsel Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic, good morning to you. Go ahead. You've got about three -- three minutes left, three to four minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to my learned friends from the Prosecution. When we addressed you first this morning we said that the liability and responsibility of Mr. Djordjevic was exaggerated. We said that his sentence is too harsh. If we step back and look at the jig-saw pieces relied on by the Trial Chamber, we would suggest that at most it shows a man who did too little rather than somebody who had a criminal intent. A man remote from the chaos others created and who indeed tried to cover things up. His role was only but a small one. We submit that the significant errors of law and fact including a lack of reasoned opinion for his convictions renders the trial judgement invalid and all counts must be quashed with Mr. Djordjevic as being acquitted on all counts of the indictment. If Mr. Djordjevic is to remain convicted, we suggest that the more coherent and logical approach would be under Article 7(3) of the Statute and only where he had the requisite knowledge and should have chosen a different course. We suggest that it is findings of omissions and knowledge that are the source of any guilt should rather be actions -- rather than actions and positive intent. If you are of the view that guilt remains, we would respectfully suggest that it is on a limited basis and calls and warrants a much reduced sentence. Briefly on our suggested reduction, we would suggest that the Trial Chamber's finding that Djordjevic played a more crucial role than Lukic, Pavkovic, Sainovic, does not stack up. It is concerning conclusion given that Djordjevic's trial judgement did not even scrutinise the role of those persons in any detail, nor did it systematically consider their role in the JCE. Although Djordjevic's role perhaps merits criticism, he is far less implicit in the Kosovo war in 1999 than this trial judgement concluded. There are clear errors of law and fact in the judgement which we respectfully ask the Appeals Chamber to rectify with a significant reduction of the sentence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djurdjic. Now we move to the response by the Prosecution -- yes. Yes, Judge Tuzmukhamedov has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TUZMUKHAMEDOV
utterances.text: Thank you. I would ask the question and then would leave it to the discretion of the lead counsel to decide who of his able colleagues would be most fit to handle it, and the question is like this: At paragraph 2134 of the Trial Chamber, the Trial Chamber -- of the trial judgement, the Trial Chamber concludes that the evidence confirms that a joint criminal enterprise involving your client was established by mid-January 1999. And then further the judgement states that this JCE may well have existed before that time. So my question is two-fold. The first layer or part of this question is: Can you direct me or the Bench to anywhere in the trial judgement where the Trial Chamber found it proven beyond reasonable doubt that a JCE involving your client existed prior to mid-January 1999? And the second layer or second part of that question is: If the answer to the first question is negative, then can you direct me to any instances in the trial judgement where the Trial Chamber imposed criminal liability on your client stemming from events occurring prior to mid-January 1999? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOPKINS
utterances.text: Dealing with the first part of your question first, the Trial Chamber's conclusion at the paragraph you referred to is that the -- the only conclusion it could ultimately reach was that the earliest the JCE existed was January 1999. That's as high as the Trial Chamber put it, so not before that date. And I know, of course, that a similar issue and similar questions were addressed in the Sainovic appeal. But in Djordjevic's case, moving to the second question about whether or not he is convicted on the basis of his conduct prior to the existence of the JCE, the answer to your question is an unequivocal yes. If you look even just at the contents pages of the judgement, for example, and you see the Trial Chamber's findings on Djordjevic's role and knowledge running from page 733 to page 781 -- the section finishes at page 787, excuse me. The first five or six sections of that trial judgement's findings all relate to events in 1998. And it does, we say, result in a logical impossibility that you just cannot participate in a JCE before it exists. Now, of course knowledge from 1998 could be used, for example, as a means to infer a similar knowledge or intent in the later period, but there's no way the conduct from the earlier period can be said to mean that one person is participating in events that happened after that. And I would rely, for example, to make good that submission, if you look at, say, the Nuremberg judgement, said to be one of the sources of JCE and customary international law, albeit we've challenged that in our appeal brief, you do not see, for example, the banker Schacht convicted of events during the war or the aggressive war. And why do you not? Because all of his conduct was pre-war or the vast majority of his conduct was pre-war, financing the Nazi rearmament regime. If you could rely on events before the JCE is created, you would not see Schacht acquitted. So that was my answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TUZMUKHAMEDOV
utterances.text: Thank you, counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Yes, good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: My name is Kyle Wood. I will provide the Prosecution's overall response to General Djordjevic's appeal and I will also answer Your Honours' first question relating to his authority as assistant minister of the interior. I will answer Your Honours' third question, which deals with deportation. My colleague Ms. Verrall will then rise to assist Your Honours with your second and fifth questions relating to aiding and abetting. And then with the remaining time, I'll deal with Your Honours' fourth question about the indictment. Now, turning then to our response. Despite, Your Honours, what you've heard this morning, the Chamber reasonably found that General Vlastimir Djordjevic was one of the most crucial members of a joint criminal enterprise that unleashed an 88-day campaign of terror and extreme violence against Kosovo Albanians, a campaign that left at least 724 people dead, that displaced hundreds of thousands of people, and that reduced many Kosovo Albanian villages to smoking ruins. Now, contrary to Djordjevic's arguments, both here and in his brief, the Chamber was reasonable to conclude that he played a key role in co-ordinating the work of the forces at the heart of this campaign in 1998 and in 1999. As Your Honours know, he gave badges to notoriously criminal paramilitaries, that's the Skorpions; he sent them to Kosovo and he gave them guns, and I will address that further. Further, he played a leading role, as you've heard, in the clandestine operations to hide the bodies of hundreds of murdered Kosovo Albanian civilians at facilities that he controlled, in an operation that he directed. And he made sure that nobody would ever be punished for the crimes that he knew his subordinates were committing in Kosovo. Now, these are the key factors, the key contributions, Your Honours, to his conviction. In challenging these findings, as you've heard this morning, Djordjevic generally rehashes his failed trial argument, in which he tries to place blame both above him and below him in the chain of command by portraying himself as a colonel-general without any power and as a commander without any authority. The Trial Chamber, Your Honours, heard this evidence, they considered this evidence, and they rejected it based on the totality of the evidence before them, based on a detailed analysis of the entire trial record. Here, on appeal, in both his brief and this morning, he has failed to show the Chamber's findings were those that no reasonable Trial Chamber could reach. As Your Honours have held repeatedly and as was repeated today this morning at the beginning of this hearing, an appeal is not a trial de novo. It's not a chance for him to run his trial arguments again for a second go. Rather, he has a burden to meet on appeal and he's failed to meet that burden. To put the arguments of the Defence in a proper context and in response to them, I'll focus today on three critical areas that were essential to the conviction of General Djordjevic - his role and contributions to the JCE, his knowledge of crimes, and his intent that they be committed. Now, first turning to his role and his contributions, contrary to what he argues to his brief and what you've heard here today, the Chamber reasonably found that Djordjevic exercised enormous authority throughout the indictment period. That's in 1998 and in 1999. And of course, the Prosecution accepts that the indictment period for the purposes of the crimes is January to June 1999. In his challenge to the Chamber's findings regarding his role, he repeats his failed argument from trial that in 1999 he was essentially robbed of any authority over the RJB units on the ground. Now, in rejecting this argument, the Trial Chamber pointed to the myriad of specific examples of the way in which Djordjevic continued to exercise authority in 1999, including most critically between -- in the indictment period. I'll highlight some of these now, findings that you generally haven't heard about from today's -- this morning's presentation. Specifically, the Chamber found that he played a role in planning and co-ordinating the work of the MUP and VJ forces in Kosovo, that's at 2154; that he contributed to the deployment of paramilitary units in Kosovo, including, but not limited to, the Skorpions unit in March 1999; he played a leading role in efforts to conceal murders by moving corpses from Kosovo and hiding them in graves in facilities in Serbia that he controlled; and he failed to take any measures to ensure a proper investigation. Turning first to his role in co-ordinating the work of the MUP forces in 1999. The evidence shows that there was plainly, Your Honours, a plan in -- for -- that the MUP was planning a large-scale offensive in the spring of 1999 and this is critical to Djordjevic's contributions. During a 17 February 1999 meeting in the MUP staff in Pristina in which Djordjevic also attended, Stojiljkovic, who was the minister of the interior, said: "Within two or three days of an attack by NATO, we have to put our plans in motion and use the time to clear the territory of terrorists." That's at paragraph 2020. Critically, Stojiljkovic also said that his subordinates were to "approach and engage volunteers carefully, linking their engagement through the reserve police force when assessed as necessary." The evidence shows and the Chamber reasonably found that General Djordjevic played a key role in executing this plan. He remained a member of the Joint Command throughout 1999. Further, he was a member of the MUP collegium, Your Honours. That's at paragraph 2154 of the trial judgement. As Your Honours will recall, the MUP collegium was a forum in which requests were received for approval of additional units being sent to Kosovo and in which anti-terrorist operations were discussed in detail. That's at paragraph 1989. And of course, he deployed a paramilitary unit, the Skorpions, to Kosovo on 28 March 1999 that massacred 14 women and children. Your Honours should further note the Chamber also found that he was involved in deploying other units to Kosovo in the same time-period, and this is, of course, leading up to the campaign that was unleashed on the 24th of March at the same time the NATO bombing campaign began. For example, trial judgement paragraph 61 lists a number of instances in which Djordjevic deployed PJP or special police units to Kosovo for various purposes generally described as "for the purpose of carrying out special security tasks in Kosovo." And as you'll see in paragraph 61, these orders happened throughout March and into April, including on 18 March, on 21 March, on 23 March, on 24 March. This is further evidence, Your Honours, of Djordjevic's role in the plan that the MUP was plainly putting together for the operation that would become the campaign of terror and extreme violence that are the subject of the crimes with which he is charged. Turning specifically to paramilitaries, now as I've explained, in a 17 February 1999 meeting of the MUP staff, General Stojiljkovic said his subordinates were to engage and -- approach and engage volunteers carefully, that is, to prepare for their use. On 18 February, the very next day, Djordjevic sent a dispatch telling his subordinates to "establish complete control over volunteer and paramilitary units and their members." Now, this is important to understand in the context of the deployment of the Skorpions, Your Honour. It was the Skorpions and the deployment of that unit with which he was most personally involved. Now, the Chamber found that he essentially solicited their use, their service. That's at paragraph 1935. The Chamber found that he made sure they got MUP badges. That's at paragraph 1942. That he would make sure that they would get bussed to Kosovo where they were given uniforms and guns. That's at paragraph 1937. As Your Honours know, the Chamber also found he knew the unit had a reputation for criminal violence from its fighting in Kosovo [sic]. And that's at paragraph 1953. Now, how did he know that? The Chamber's finding on this point was reasonable, Your Honours, based on a number of factors. First of all, I take you back to paragraph 1935 of the trial judgement in which the Chamber found he told K92 to gather Medic's men. And according to the testimony of Trajkovic, who was the commander of the anti-terrorist police which is the unit to which the Skorpions would eventually be attached to, it was well-known that the Skorpions were always referred to as a distinct unit, as the Skorpions. It's also clear that he knew that they were volunteer -- that there were paramilitary -- a paramilitary unit and that he knew and in the defining of -- I'm sorry, in Djordjevic's own words, he knew that paramilitary units were oftentimes a front for criminal interests, and that's in his testimony at paragraph -- transcript T 945 [sic]. And of course he knew about their prior experience in Croatia. And it's also important to know -- that's at, I'm sorry, transcript T 9696 to 9697. And it's also important to note, Your Honour, that the Chamber found that the Skorpions had previously been engaged with a different unit of the MUP, the other arm, if you will, the DB, when they were engaged in Croatia. Nevertheless, as the Chamber found, he failed to engage in any criminal background checks of these units. That's clear, Your Honours, from the findings of the Trial Chamber regardless of whether they would have found a criminal background from Croatia. What is clear is that no criminal background checks were done whatsoever and what is also clear in the finding of the Chamber is that this was an obligation of Djordjevic. Under the law, as a police officer, if he's going to give a group of men authority as police officers, badges, guns, and send them particularly into an area of inter-ethnic hostility, he's required under the law to make sure that these men are worthy of that privilege. And it's plain that he did not in this case. Now, as Your Honours know, the Skorpions were responsible for the massacre of 14 women and children shortly after they arrived in Podujevo on 28 March 1999. It found that Djordjevic was informed about this massacre almost immediately by a telephone from his subordinate. Now, rather than investigate this incident and hold the perpetrators accountable, he actively thwarted -- in the finding of the Chamber, to thwart any probe into the killings. As the Chamber found in paragraph 1957, he took no disciplinary action upon hearing of this massacre. There was no follow-up on the 30 March 1999 report until May 1999, and even then, Your Honours, of course it's important to note that May 1999 is after the Skorpions had already been redeployed into Kosovo, even then only two perpetrators were detained and even then for only ten days. And as the Defence said this morning, there was -- nobody was prosecuted for these crimes during the tenure of Djordjevic. Even though it is clear in the finding of the Chamber at trial judgement paragraph 196 that it was Djordjevic and the MUP who were responsible for the paramilitaries and who were responsible for making sure they would be punished or that the incident would be investigated fully. Here today Djordjevic fails to show these findings were those that no reasonable Trial Chamber could have made. Here, as in other instances in his arguments, he seeks to substitute his own evaluation of the evidence for that of the Trial Chamber. And in his brief I'll note he seeks to rely specifically on the evidence of two witnesses that the Chamber listened to, evaluated, and rejected as not being credible. He seeks to rely on these same witnesses who -- for the argument that the perpetrators of these crimes were not redeployed to Kosovo afterward. The Chamber found that this was also not believable, Your Honours. It found that all but one of the men were redeployed to Kosovo in April 1999. That's at paragraphs 1964 and 1965 of the judgement. And that's not surprising, considering the poor investigation or lack of investigation that had been carried out into this massacre and to those who were -- who might be responsible for it. And contrary to what the Defence argues today, he was not convicted of any crimes that they committed afterwards, but it is noteworthy that a member of the Skorpions -- that another soldier remembered -- described seeing them in the presence of fleeing villages -- of villages that were burning and with villagers fleeing from those villages. Now, turning next to the concealment of bodies, it's important to note, Your Honours, that Djordjevic himself admitted involvement in this incident. And when I say "incident," really what I mean is a month-long clandestine operation that involved digging up bodies of hundreds of murdered Kosovo Albanians, transporting them hundreds of miles into Serbia, and burying them in facilities controlled by Djordjevic's RJB. He knew these victims were Kosovo Albanians, some of whom had been murdered by MUP officers, and he also said that he knew it was shameful and wrong to bury them in this way. And I refer Your Honours to paragraphs 1973 -- paragraph 1973 of the trial judgement and various places in the trial testimony of General Djordjevic, for example, T 9723, 9727, 9730 to 9733, 9821, 10002, 10004, 10006, and 10008 through 11. And you should see on your screen now, Your Honours, a couple of those admissions. General Djordjevic said: "I knew then as I know now that it wasn't right, and I'm willing to assume responsibility for a rash action." And of course the evidence shows that this was anything but a rash action but something that took place over the period of weeks as the campaign of terror and violence was being committed in Kosovo. Another quote, if I can move to the next slide. If Your Honours are ready. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: The next quote he said, he told the Chamber: "I'm aware this was a big mistake I made, but what happened cannot be made undone. I am ashamed of my deeds and I believe that the Court's decision will be adequate and I will be held responsible for what I did." Now, the Chamber's finding that Djordjevic was -- directed this campaign, that he may have been the main orchestrator of the burial of the bodies at Batajnica, it's consistent with all the evidence. The Chamber found based on this evidence that he directed this operation in which MUP drivers, bodies -- brought bodies of more than 800 victims from Kosovo into Serbia in MUP trucks to be buried in two MUP facilities that Djordjevic controlled. This is the Batajnica SAJ or anti-terrorist police training centre and the Petrovo Selo PJP or special police centre. The Chamber found that he was the one person in charge of all the MUP personnel involved. That's at paragraph 2118. And that he even personally chose the grave-sites of where the bodies should be buried when they arrived at Batajnica. Before each truck arrived he told the person who was there to deal with the bodies, that it was coming, and what to do with it. When he was told that the murders -- that the bodies had been discovered in Tekija and in Lake Perucac, he told his subordinates to cover up those crimes. He told his subordinates to destroy the refrigerated truck that had been found in the Danube, and he even authorised payment of 10.000 dinars to those who were involved. Now, this is an important contribution the Chamber found. Contrary to what you've heard this is not an ex post facto covering up of crime. It was a contribution because it happened during the time that the campaign of violence and terror was being unleashed on Kosovo Albanians. In fact, the Chamber found even that Djordjevic was in Kosovo in April 1999 at the same time that the campaign was happening, at the same time that this operation of hiding bodies was also ongoing. You've heard also, turning to knowledge and intent, Your Honours, in the brief, that Djordjevic tries to portray himself as a man who was cut off, that he had no idea of what was happening in Kosovo, but of course the Chamber found differently and that's based on the evidence and based on something you heard even this morning, Your Honours. The Chamber found that he was notified through oral reports of his subordinates, through the media, through his personal observations. And as the Defence noted this morning or as the appellant noted this morning, he was informed almost immediately of the massacres at Podujevo by telephone. Despite this knowledge of things that were happening in Kosovo, he did nothing to investigate, did nothing to stop. This showed, Your Honours, that he did have the intent that these crimes be committed, his continued involvement in the JCE. Now, with this context in mind, Your Honours, I'll turn to answering Your Honours' first question. Now, I'll note in relation to the answer I heard this morning that it sounds awfully familiar and it's because the argument you heard this morning is very, very similar to the argument that the Defence tried to run at trial and it was definitively rejected by the Trial Chamber. After its evaluation of all the evidence, it came to a reasonable conclusion. Now, Your Honours asked that the questions be read into the record so I'll do that. "Discuss, in relation to Djordjevic's subground of appeal 9(A), how the areas of responsibility of Assistant Ministers Petar Zekovic and Obrad Stevanovic would overlap with, and impact on, Djordjevic's authority as Assistant Minister of Interior, and in relation to subground of appeal 9(F), Djordjevic's role in the deployment of the Skorpions." Now, contrary to what the Defence said -- to what the appellant said this morning, the Chamber did consider all the laws, they did consider all the witnesses, and what they found is that the witnesses that Djordjevic put on in support of his argument were -- or that his argument was unsupported and not credible. The Chamber reasonably found that the areas of responsibility of Zekovic and Stevanovic did not overlap with, nor impact on, Djordjevic's general authority as chief of the RJB. Though all three men were assistant ministers, Djordjevic outranked both Stevanovic and Zekovic and the Chamber reasonably found that both men headed departments that were within his RJB. Starting first with Zekovic. Now, the Chamber found, looking at Exhibit P263 and P537, that Zekovic was head of the administration for joint affairs. The administration for joint affairs, the Chamber found, was an organisational unit of the RJB. That's at paragraph 41 in Exhibit P357, Article 13. It also found that the RJB departments functioned under the control of Djordjevic. That's trial judgement paragraph 40. It's worth noting here, Your Honours, that the Defence -- the appellant offers no support for his argument that the MUP was a series of fiefdoms riven by strife and -- in tension. The Chamber found quite the opposite, that it was a hierarchical organisation in which members -- in which the general authority of Djordjevic meant that he had authority over the departments within his RJB. Similarly with Stevanovic, the Chamber found that he was chief of the police administration. That's at paragraphs 41, 60, 100, 2127, 2175. Again, it found that the police administration was a department within the RJB, at paragraphs 41 and 1936, and therefore functioned under the control of Djordjevic. And that's at paragraphs 40 and 1936. On the other hand, the Chamber found that there was no evidence to support the idea that there was any overlap, and here is where they specifically reject the Defence argument, between the specific authority of another assistant minister and the general authority of Djordjevic as chief of the RJB. That's at paragraph 43. Now, that's what the law says, Your Honours, but this is also consistent with the role that the two men played in the incidents that are relevant to this issue. Starting first with the burials of the bodies. Though Zekovic has a minor part in this operation, it was Djordjevic who was -- who directed it. That's at paragraphs 1972, 1980, 2112, 2118, and 2156 of the trial judgement. Now, again, thinking back to what it is that Djordjevic did in this operation, before each load of bodies arrived at the centre [sic], it was Djordjevic who told the personnel there that the truck was coming, that it contained bodies, and where these bodies should be buried. It was Djordjevic who told his subordinates to cover-up the discovery of the bodies at Perucac and in the refrigerated container at Tekija. When Zekovic later assigned drivers to collect bodies from Pristina, that's at paragraphs 1342 and 1535 [sic] of the judgement, and from Kosovska Mitrovica, at paragraph 1355, for burial at the Batajnica centre, he was merely playing his role in an operation that was done under the direction of Djordjevic. That's consistent with his role as head of administration for joint affairs, and it's consistent with the Chamber's finding that this is not the picture of a man whose responsibilities overlapped with those of Djordjevic. And it's the same, turning to subground 9(F), the Chamber reasonably found that it was Djordjevic who recruited the Skorpions, who saw to it they be made a reserve force and attached to the special terrorist police. It was Djordjevic who did all of these things to make sure the Skorpions were part of the MUP and sent to Podujevo. Though the Chamber found the police administration which was headed by Stevanovic would have been responsible for replenishment of the anti-terrorist police forces, that's at paragraph 1936, it also noted that it was Djordjevic who authorised this replenishment, that's at paragraphs 75, 1896, and 1936. Again Stevanovic was doing his -- playing his part in an action that was directed and controlled by Djordjevic. And that concludes my answer to Your Honours' question one. Unless you have any other further questions, I'll move on to question three.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: So question three. As Your Honours requested, I'll read that into the record. "Discuss, in relation to Djordjevic's 13th ground of appeal and with reference to the trial record, whether, for the purpose of establishing the crime of deportation and in light of customary international law, a de facto border existed between Kosovo and Montenegro during the indictment period." The short answer, Your Honours, is that the Chamber reasonably concluded based on the facts of this case that the well-established border between Kosovo and Montenegro in 1999 had the characteristics of a de facto border for the purposes of establishing the crime of deportation. Now, the trial record supports this, as I'll explain, and it's also consistent with Your Honours' holding in the Stakic appeal judgement which is the controlling case on this point and which the -- which Djordjevic today generally ignores, choosing instead to focus on dissenting opinions from other cases. Now, what's the basis on which the Chamber found that there was a de facto border? Well, it found that Kosovo was a geographically distinct, autonomous province that had previously enjoyed a tradition of autonomy and self-management within Serbia. Now, what did this mean? In the finding of the Chamber this meant -- it included the right of Kosovo Albanians to receive instruction and to address their government in a language -- in their own language. This level of self-management included a Supreme Court, a police force, and a central bank. Secondly, it found that on the other side of the border was Montenegro which was a republic with its own status within the FRY. And third, it found that as at the end of May 1998 an armed conflict existed in Kosovo between the KLA and Serbia and the FRY. The Chamber also noted that the displacement of ethnic Albanians from Kosovo to Montenegro would have much the same effect as displacement across a state border. Now, this is consistent also with the way these operations were conducted and shows that the perpetrators themselves even recognised the importance of Kosovo's border. We're talking about two instances here, Your Honour. In Kosovska Mitrovica, one of those instances, Serb forces forced Kosovo Albanians onto 16 or 17 buses of a state transport company and drove them straight to the border with Montenegro. This was an organised displacement that mirrored other organised displacements to other borders with Kosovo. And I refer Your Honours to paragraphs 777 and 1646. At the border they were maltreated, interrogated, and forced to shout "Serbia, Serbia." This is consistent with how Kosovo Albanians were treated at other borders. The perpetrators were pushing the victims across this border and telling them they were not welcome to return. They were deporting them. And for the findings in Pec, I refer Your Honours to paragraphs 732 and 734 and 1642 of the trial judgement. Given these findings, it was reasonable for the Chamber to conclude as a matter of fact that a de facto border existed between Kosovo and Montenegro and that this border shared some of the characteristics of a de jure border. Now, as I said, this is also consistent with Your Honours' approach in Stakic. Now, what does Stakic require? Stakic says that under customary international law, deportation requires the forced displacement across a border. That's at paragraph 300. And it says also that under certain circumstances this can be a de facto border. That's at 278 and 300 of the Stakic appeal judgement. It says that the determination must be made on a case-by-case basis in light of the overall elements of deportation under customary international law. That's at paragraphs 278 and 300. Now, though Stakic provides no specific indicia of what constitutes a de facto border, what it plainly doesn't do is limit this definition to areas of control as indicated by or argued by Djordjevic today. Now, applying this understanding to the trial judgement in Stakic, the Chamber found that there was no evidence to support its findings that constantly changing front lines can amount to deportation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, to be correct, I don't think that appellant alleged that Stakic referred to areas of control. It was a reference to what Judge Shahabuddeen mentioned in his dissenting opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I didn't mean to suggest that Stakic did say that or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. But you --

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: -- but the Defence suggested that it did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: To be clear, though Stakic did not lay out any indicia for what defines a de facto border, it didn't say that it depends on areas of control. Now, in this case, Your Honours, of course we're not dealing with a constantly changing front line, but a static geographic border around a well-defined territory of Kosovo. Unlike what the Trial Chamber did in Stakic, the Trial Chamber here did engage in the fact by fact -- in the case-by-case analysis that's required. Now, this finding is consistent with the values under customary international law that the crime of deportation is meant to protect, as indicated in the Stakic appeal judgement, Your Honour, that is, to protect people from being forcibly displaced and to protect their right to live in their communities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Suppose the appellant is asking us to look at Stakic anew and to see whether that decision should be reviewed, whether there are cogent reasons for departing from it. As I understand it, what counsel was saying is that the relevant criterion under customary international law is not the border, the crossing of a border, but whether the controlling power is the same. And I think he was suggesting that the controlling power in Kosovo was the same as the controlling power in Montenegro. He didn't go as far as I have suggested, but if you're correct that Stakic represents customary international law, then I would imagine that you would really have to be asking this Chamber, following the Aleksovski principle, to look at the matter afresh and to see whether that decision should be -- whether there are cogent reasons for departing from it. Now, what do you say to the stress that he has placed on this matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I don't see in his brief or in his arguments even today any clear and cogent reasons that Your Honours should depart from Stakic. Your Honours, after doing an analysis in Stakic of customary international law, defined what it meant, that is, the de facto border; that is to say, it said that a de facto border can be relevant for the purposes of deportation. Now, if Your Honours are seeking to revisit Stakic, I would suggest that you don't have the record before you to do that. Neither party has asked for Stakic to be overturned. The Defence has not or the appellant hasn't put or suggested any clear and cogent reasons to depart from Stakic. Rather, Stakic stands for the proposition that it's a case-by-case analysis in light of customary international law. In this case, the Trial Chamber did exactly as Your Honours required in Stakic which is conduct that case-by-case analysis. It's not a question of whether Stakic is wrong but whether the analysis that this Trial Chamber did in concluding that there was a de facto border was, in fact, a correct one. And in the submission of the Prosecution, the appellant has failed to show that this finding was unreasonable under the specific facts of this case for the specific purpose of determining whether deportation was committed in these two municipalities. And I would, just to conclude, Your Honours, very quickly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You still have another 10, 11, 12 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Okay. That in this case, regardless of -- regardless of whether you find error in this case -- or let me back up. There's two issues that are important here. The first is: What is the proper labelling of this conduct criminally? And the second is: What effect does it have on the judgement? Now, dealing with the first issue, even if you find that the Trial Chamber erred in fact in concluding that this was a de facto border, you should find that the forcible displacement to Montenegro from these two municipalities constituted forcible transfer. This is the approach Your Honours took in the Stakic appeal judgement at paragraph 321. And even Djordjevic recognises at paragraph 98 [Realtime transcript read in error "28"] of his reply brief, and I think he repeated it here today, that these acts would constitute the crime of forcible transfer but for this question of the border between Kosovo and Montenegro. So Your Honours have the power to do that. Secondly, regardless of whether you label the displacements here deportations or forcible transfer, the Prosecution points out that they remain acts of persecution under Djordjevic's conviction for persecutions as a crime against humanity. Now, as Your Honours have held repeatedly for the purposes of persecutions, it's irrelevant whether the underlying act was deportation or whether it was forcible transfer. Either one suffices so long as the act was carried out with a requisite discriminatory intent. And of course, in this case, Your Honours, the findings show that they were. And for the law on that I would refer you to Naletilic and Martinovic appeal judgement paragraph 154. So to conclude question three, the Appeals Chamber should affirm the Trial Chamber 's finding that in this case based on these facts, Kosovo Albanians driven from Kosovska Mitrovica and from Pec were deported. Alternatively, it should find that they were forcibly transferred and it should adjust Djordjevic's sentence in accordance with the Prosecution's appeal. And that concludes my answer to Your Honours' question three. Unless you have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I'm just noting the time, Your Honour, and at this point, as I suggested, I would turn the podium over -- the lectern over to my colleague Ms. Verrall. Perhaps given how close we are to the break, it might be best just to break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We could do that of course, but you won't get any extra time. Because, as you know, post-break schedule is conditioned by my need to leave at 3.00 for this meeting. So I suggest you still have a few minutes, you start.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VERRALL
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. VERRALL
utterances.text: I will be addressing numbers two and five of Your Honours' questions, both of which relate to Djordjevic's convictions through aiding and abetting as a mode of liability. Your Honours, I would turn first to question five, namely, why convictions through both JCE and aiding and abetting, based on the same contributions, better reflect the totality of Djordjevic's conduct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's two, not five, no? Oh, no, okay, you're correct. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VERRALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, convicting Djordjevic through both forms of liability concurrently enabled the Trial Chamber to emphasise his high level of culpability, pairing the higher mens rea requirement from JCE with the higher actus reus contribution from aiding and abetting. And it also enabled the Trial Chamber to emphasise those aspects of Djordjevic's conduct that had the most direct link to the crimes and provided substantial support to the perpetrators. Your Honours, at this point I would note the Prosecution disagrees with the submission by my learned friend this morning for the Defence that the conducts taken into account for both JCE and aiding and abetting is entirely the same. As we see it, four types of contribution are taken into account for JCE and those are, very briefly, Djordjevic's role in planning and co-ordinating MUP operations, his role in deploying the Skorpions and other volunteer units, the concealment of bodies, and then, fourthly, his failure to prevent and punish crimes. But when one looks at the findings on aiding and abetting, the Chamber only relies on the final three of those. And in our submission, Your Honour, that is important because it shows the Trial Chamber adopted this approach because it wanted to place an emphasis on a particular part of Djordjevic's conduct. And, Your Honours, this approach is consistent with the Trial Chamber's view of Djordjevic's high level of culpability and his active role in facilitating crimes. In the Chamber's finding, and I quote, "no other member of the joint criminal enterprise made a more crucial contribution to the achievement of its objective." And I would refer Your Honours to paragraph 2211 of the trial judgement. Your Honours, contrary to Djordjevic's submissions this morning that convicting through concurrent modes somehow violates his right to a clear articulation of his criminal responsibility, the Trial Chamber has in fact very clearly and transparently set out his criminal responsibility in a precise manner. There is nothing logically inconsistent about convicting for these two modes of responsibility concurrently. We acknowledge they are distinct modes but they are not mutually exclusively or logically incompatible, and the fact that they cover some of the same conduct does not alter the issue of whether concurrent modes are permissible. Ultimately, Your Honours, this was a matter of discretion for the Trial Chamber. We acknowledge it did not need to adopt this approach, but it convicted through both modes in the interests of clarity and completeness. And Djordjevic can point to no prejudice arising from this approach. Your Honours, I wish to touch very briefly on the jurisprudence that enables convictions under concurrent modes under Article 7(1) of the Statute. Now, in convicting Djordjevic through these concurrent modes, the Trial Chamber relied on three appellate cases which my learned friend has mentioned this morning, Ndindabahizi, Kamuhanda, and Nahimana, and all of these cases recognise that an accused can be convicted on the basis of concurrent modes of liability. Your Honours, I wish to highlight the Ndindabahizi appeal judgement. It confirms that it is possible to convict based on more than one mode even when, as in the present case, the conduct that forms the basis of those modes partially overlaps. Now, that case, Your Honours, dealt with convictions through the concurrent modes of commission, aiding and abetting, and instigation. And specifically, the words of encouragement that formed part of the appellate Ndindabahizi's conviction for commission was exactly the same conduct that was taken into account for aiding and abetting and instigation. And the Appeals Chamber found no error in that approach because it accepted that the Trial Chamber was seeking to provide a further characterisation of the accused's conduct.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Kindly slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VERRALL
utterances.text: Thank you. And I would refer Your Honours to paragraphs 122 and 123 of the appeal judgement. Your Honours, I plan to break in just one minute but if I can perhaps just conclude on the Ndindabahizi appeals judgement. In our submission, that case is also important not only because it deals with overlapping conduct but because it is a case of commission. And my learned friend this morning has placed quite some emphasis on the apparent incompatibility in this case between convicting through JCE as a primary mode and aiding and abetting as a secondary or accomplice liability. We simply note that in the Ndindabahizi appeals judgement, that seemed to be acceptable in the eyes of the Appeals Chamber. And perhaps it is a convenient time to break, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. We will reconvene at 2.00. Thank you. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.40 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So good afternoon to everyone. We'll continue, Madam. We will stop a little bit before 3.00 for the meeting that I have and then we continue after that hour break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VERRALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. To continue with my response to question five on concurrent convictions, Your Honours, just before the break I had finished outlining why the Ndindabahizi appeals judgement is an illustrative case in this instance. In the interests of time, I don't propose to go into the Kamuhanda and Nahimana judgements but note that those cases also further support the proposition that multiple modes of liability are permissible. But, Your Honours, I do wish to address the Bench on the separate opinion of Judge Schomburg in Kamuhanda. And although the Defence didn't raise that this morning, I want to address it because it really goes to the heart of some of the issues that have been raised by the Defence. Your Honours, if one looks at the separate opinion of Judge Schomburg in Kamuhanda and particularly at paragraph 389, it seems that his position was the view that an accused should not be punished twice for the same conduct under two heads of liability, and in our respectful submission, this concern is based on a misplaced premise. In convicting through more than one mode of liability, the accused is still only convicted once for the crime in question. Your Honours, I would pause at this moment to also address the Akayesu trial judgement which the Defence raised this morning, and in particular, they pointed to paragraph 468 where the Trial Chamber in that case indicated it was inappropriate to convict an accused of two offences when one is accomplice liability and the other is principal liability. Your Honour, again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. Go back to the point that you made in relation to Judge Schomburg. You have sought to correct Judge Schomburg's approach by saying that in convicting on more than one mode of liability, the accused is still only convicted once for the crime in question. But the question of punishment might be different. How is that reflected in sentence?

utterances.speaker: MS. VERRALL
utterances.text: Your Honour, in our submission, there is no prejudice in this approach in convicting through two concurrent modes because if we look at the present case, it is clear that the principle that guided the Trial Chamber was the totality of Djordjevic's conduct. We can see in the disposition section of the judgement that he is, in fact, convicted only once for each crime in question. And then the Trial Chamber clearly sets out at paragraph 2214 of the judgement, and I'll quote: "In the view of the Chamber, in the circumstances of this case, the sentence appropriate for the leading and grave role of the Accused in the joint criminal enterprise and in aiding and abetting the offences established, fully and adequately reflect the totality of the criminality of the Accused which warrants punishment. It will determine the sentence accordingly." In summary, Your Honours, we consider that there is no prejudice in this approach because at the end of the day, the Trial Chamber looked at the totality of Djordjevic's conduct and it sentenced him on that basis. Does that answer Your Honour's question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I'm happy with it. I was just trying to put in a context an approach that I thought was fairer to what Judge Schomburg was saying.

utterances.speaker: MS. VERRALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. To return very briefly to the point I was making earlier, and that is just to clarify the Akayesu trial judgement, and again, the comments made in that case were in relation to cumulative convictions, and the example given by the Trial Chamber was that it would be inappropriate to convict for both genocide and complicity in genocide. And we acknowledge, Your Honours, that the concerns in terms of cumulative convictions are quite different and perhaps there may be more concern of double punishment when it comes to cumulative convictions. But here, we are concerned squarely with convicting through concurrent modes. To conclude on this point, Your Honours, imposing convictions through concurrent modes was a matter for the Trial Chamber's discretion. Djordjevic was only convicted once under Article 7(1) for each crime for which he is guilty and he was appropriately sentenced based on the totality of his conduct. Your Honours, there is no prejudice in this approach. Accordingly, we would ask the Appeals Chamber to dismiss Djordjevic's 18th ground of appeal as it relates to convictions through concurrent modes of responsibility. Your Honours, I now turn to question two which also relates to Djordjevic's responsibility for aiding and abetting crimes. Your Honours have asked us to discuss, first, the implications of the Trial Chamber not making explicit findings on substantial contribution in relation to the crime of forcible transfer. And second, the implications of the Trial Chamber not making explicit findings on specific direction for aiding and abetting generally. And, Your Honours, I will answer the two parts of this question in turn. First, turning to the lack of a finding in relation to the requirement of substantial effect for aiding and abetting the crime of forcible transfer. To summarise our position, Your Honours, while the Trial Chamber omitted to make this specific finding, this omission has no impact on the conviction. In considering aiding and abetting liability, the Trial Chamber had previously set out the correct elements, including the requirement of substantial effect, and this can be found at paragraph 1874. The two critical paragraphs for the purposes of this question, Your Honours, are, as the Defence have pointed out this morning, paragraphs 2163 and 2164. I don't propose to read through those, Your Honours, but when those two critical paragraphs are read side by side, it is evident that the Trial Chamber simply omitted to include the words "forcible transfer" when reaching its conclusions on substantial effect. As I've mentioned, it was mindful of the correct standard to be applied. It applied it with respect to the other remaining crimes and, indeed, it intended to convict Djordjevic for aiding and abetting forcible transfers. This omission, to the extent that it could be called an error, does not have any impact on Djordjevic's convictions for forcible transfer through aiding and abetting. Your Honours, there are sufficient findings within the judgement to fulfil the substantial effect requirement. And it is within the scope of the Appeals Chamber's powers to uphold this conviction based on those remaining findings. And in this respect I would refer Your Honours to the recent appeal judgement in Lukic and Lukic, paragraph 437, where the Appeals Chamber upheld a conviction for aiding and abetting where the Trial Chamber had similarly omitted to make a specific finding on substantial effect. Your Honours, in the present case, the starting point is the finding of substantial effect in relation to the other proven crimes. The Trial Chamber was satisfied that Djordjevic's conduct had a substantial effect on the crimes of murder, persecutions, and deportation. Now, in particular, that conduct was comprised of his failure to investigate or punish crimes committed by his subordinates; his leading role in efforts to actively conceal crimes including through the transportation and mass burial of bodies; and his personal role in deploying volunteers and paramilitary units into Kosovo. Your Honours, to understand how these contributions had a substantial effect on the crimes, we need to look at the context in which the crimes occurred. These crimes occurred as part of a widespread campaign of terror and extreme violence that caused Kosovo Albanians to flee from their homes. Djordjevic's actions directly facilitated and perpetuated this campaign, and thus his actions had a substantial effect on the crimes that occurred as a result of it. In particular, Your Honours, to the extent that his actions had a substantial effect on the crime of deportation, they must necessarily have the same substantial effect on the crime of forcible transfer, because it was the same campaign that forced Kosovo Albanians from their homes and villages in both instances. The only difference between these crimes was whether or not there was proof that the victims crossed a border. Djordjevic's contributions and the effects that they had on the crimes in both instances are the same. To conclude, Your Honours, the Trial Chamber simply omitted to enter a finding of substantial effect in relation to aiding and abetting forcible transfer, but this has no impact on the verdict. When Djordjevic's contributions are understood as impacting on the entire campaign of terror and violence, a reasonable trier of fact would be entitled to find that his actions had a substantial effect on all of the crimes that were part and parcel of that campaign. Your Honours, the findings in the trial judgement are sufficient to sustain a finding of substantial effect for forcible transfer, equally alongside the existing findings for deportation, murders, and persecutions. Your Honours, I will now move to address the second part of the question, namely, the implications of the Chamber's failure to make explicit findings in relation to specific direction for aiding and abetting. Your Honours, before continuing, I note that the issue of specific direction is currently before the Appeals Chamber in the Sainovic proceedings in relation to the appellant Lazarevic. In the appeals hearing in March of this year, the Prosecution set out why it considers there are cogent reasons to depart from the appeals judgement in Perisic, which recently found that specific direction is an element of aiding and abetting. Your Honours, given that aiding and abetting is not such a central issue in the present case, I do not propose to reiterate the Prosecution's stance on cogent reasons to depart from Perisic in full here today. However, if Your Honours would benefit from hearing those arguments, we would be happy to file supplemental submissions on the issue, giving both parties the opportunity to present their views in full. But if I may briefly summarise our position for the record. The Prosecution's stance on why the Perisic appeal judgement is not good law is based on four grounds. Firstly, the specific direction requirement articulated in the Perisic appeals judgement has no basis in customary international law. Secondly, it is inconsistent with the prior jurisprudence of this Tribunal. Third, it imposes a vague and unworkable legal standard. And fourth, it ultimately undermines the principles of IHL through creating an accountability gap. Your Honours, without conceding our position on cogent reasons to depart from the appeals judgement in Perisic, if this appeals judgement is to remain the authoritative law on aiding and abetting, and if that reasoning is applied to the present case, then the Trial Chamber's failure to make explicit findings on specific direction does not undermine the verdict. The Trial Chamber was not required to enter explicit findings on specific direction. This is because the Perisic appeals judgement only requires explicit findings to be entered with respect to remote aiders and abettors and that is not the case with Djordjevic. There is, therefore, no error in the Trial Chamber's approach. The Perisic appeals judgement holds that in the case of those who are proximate to the crimes, specific direction can be demonstrated implicitly through a discussion of the other elements of aiding and abetting, such as the accused's substantial contribution to the crime. In such cases, the culpable link which is denoted by the term "specific direction" will be self-evident. And I refer Your Honours to paragraphs 37 to 39 of the Perisic appeal judgement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One question. In other words, do I understand you well that, in your opinion, what was stated by the Defence, namely, that at the relevant time Djordjevic was in Belgrade and not in Kosovo, has no relevance or importance for your argument?

utterances.speaker: MS. VERRALL
utterances.text: Your Honours, I propose to go through now a number of reasons why we consider Perisic [sic] is not a remote aider and abettor and he is a proximate one. I simply note, however, that geographical remoteness is only one consideration that the Perisic Appeals Chamber noted. And in Perisic, the Appeals Chamber found that specific direction need not be considered explicitly because Perisic was -- sorry, needed to be considered explicitly because Perisic was remote. And in doing so, it relied on these factual indicators which can be found at paragraph 42 of the Perisic appeal judgement. And in that case, the VRS, the army which perpetrated the relevant crimes, were independent of the VJ, the army in which Perisic held his position. The two armies were based in separate geographical regions, indeed separate countries. The Trial Chamber also did not refer to any evidence that Perisic was physically present when criminal acts were planned or committed. Your Honours, in contrast, Djordjevic simply does not fall into the category of a remote aider and abettor. He had de jure powers and exercised effective control over the police in Kosovo, trial judgement paragraph 2154. Indeed, the Trial Chamber found that he had the highest responsibility for the principal perpetrators of the campaign, trial judgement paragraphs 2210 to 2211. He had detailed knowledge of events on the ground and he was closely involved in operational decisions in Kosovo, including through the MUP collegium and the Joint Command bodies, trial judgement paragraph 2154. As my colleague Mr. Wood has already discussed, he directly engaged volunteer units and paramilitaries and deployed them to Kosovo. In particular, he personally facilitated the deployment of the notorious paramilitary group, the Skorpions, trial judgement paragraphs 1934 to 1966. He was also intimately connected to the crimes on the ground. In an effort to conceal the killings that occurred as part of this campaign, he gave direct orders for the clandestine transportation and reburial of bodies in mass graves. Your Honours, I would pause to emphasise at this point that the concealment of bodies is not an ex post facto contribution to aiding and abetting. That is not how the Prosecution framed this case and nor is that how the Trial Chamber has dealt with it. Therefore, in our submissions, the submissions made by the Defence this morning outlining the need for a prior agreement in cases of ex post facto aiding and abetting are not on point. The concealment operation was a continuing contribution which lasted throughout the campaign. It was a contribution because it allowed the campaign to continue unhindered and unchecked and outside the purview of international observers. Returning to why Djordjevic is proximate to the crimes, he was also present on the ground in Kosovo including when crimes were committed. For instance, he was the most senior MUP official at the Racak operation in mid-January 1999 where not less than 45 Kosovo Albanians were killed. Your Honours, this is not a charged crime but it was reasonably taken into account by the Trial Chamber to note the start date of the JCE, and we submit it is equally relevant to showing Djordjevic's intimate connection to events on the ground in Kosovo and his knowledge of crimes. Your Honours, the same factors that I have just outlined to show why Djordjevic is a proximate aider and abettor also implicitly demonstrate the existence of what the Perisic appeals judgement calls a culpable link between his actions and the crimes, due to his intimate connection to the events on the ground. Your Honours, the Trial Chamber was not required to enter explicit findings on specific direction because Djordjevic is not a remote aider and abettor. There is therefore no error. On the approach set out in the Perisic appeal judgement, the existence of a culpable link is implicit in other findings of the judgement, particularly those that go to his substantial effect on the crimes. For these reasons, we ask that the Appeals Chamber uphold Djordjevic's convictions for aiding and abetting. Unless Your Honours have any questions in relation to the aiding and abetting grounds I have discussed, I would yield the floor to my colleague Mr. Wood who would continue with the remainder of our response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Yes, good afternoon, Your Honours. Before I get into the answer to question four, I have a few corrections to the transcript, and if it's convenient, I could do that now. Transcript line 66 -- transcript 66, line 24, it says "Kosovo," it should say "Croatia." Transcript 67, line 11, it should be T 9545, that's a transcript reference. At transcript 70, lines 4 to 5, it occurs to me that I neglected to put into the record the transcript references for the slides that I showed, so at lines 4 and 5 that should be T 10009 to T 10010. And at lines 13 to 16 on transcript page 70, it should be transcript 10006. At transcript 74, line 7, the word "Batajnica" should appear before "centre." And at transcript 80, line 11, it should be 98 of the reply brief, not 28. And finally, just noticed at transcript 92, line 16, it should read "Djordjevic," not "Perisic." Now, with that out of the way, I'll turn to the answer to question four. Your Honours, the Trial Chamber did not err in convicting General Djordjevic based on the incidents that you have specified in question four. Each of these incidents falls within the time-period charged in the indictment, within the geographic area charged in the indictment, and within the widespread and systematic attack on Kosovo Albanians described in the indictment. Any ambiguity there may have been about the specific incidents noted in question four was cured because the Prosecution provided Djordjevic with timely, clear, and consistent information detailing the factual basis which underpinned the charges against him. This is consistent with Your Honours' holding in the Naletilic/Martinovic appeal judgement at paragraphs 26 and 27. The Prosecution further notes that Djordjevic has failed to show that his ability to prepare his defence was materially impaired by any of the defects he alleges in ground 16. He's raising these objections for the first time here before Your Honours on appeal. He didn't raise a specific objection at trial when the relevant evidence was introduced. This means, Your Honours, that he bears the burden of proving that the defect in the indictment that he alleges materially impaired his ability to prepare his defence. And that's Your Honours' holding in the Simic appeal judgement at paragraph 25. What this means, Your Honours, is that Djordjevic must provide specific information about how his defence was materially impaired by the alleged lack of notice such as indicating, for example, how particular witnesses would have been engaged differently, including the specific questions he would have asked, and establishing precisely how his approach to the case would have differed from the approach which he, in fact, adopted. And that's from the Mrksic appeal judgement at paragraph 144. In this case, Djordjevic has failed to meet this burden. Rather, he merely provides a list of alleged defects in the indictment without providing any information about how these defects materially impaired his ability to prepare his defence. And that's in his appeal brief at paragraphs 357 to 360. He did not object when evidence of these incidents was introduced. He cross-examined many of the relevant witnesses. And in the case of the murders at Pusto Selo, he called a witness and put on evidence to rebut evidence of this incident. I'll explain that more -- further in a bit. Now, all of this shows that Djordjevic was put on notice of the Prosecution's case and able to respond to those allegations, consistent with Your Honours' holding at Naletilic paragraph 27. Now, to explain this further, I'll go through each of these incidents in order. Now, starting first with the deportation from Kladernica village between 12 and 15 April, that's in subpart (a) of question four. The displacement from Kladernica was specifically pled at paragraph 72(c) of the indictment. Further specificity about this incident, including that the deportations occurred between 12 and 15 April 1999, was provided in the Prosecution's pre-trial submissions, including its 65 ter witness summary of Sadik Januzi which was filed on the 1st of September, 2008. And that's the same date that all of the 65 ter summaries that I'll be referring to was filed, Your Honour. Further specificity was provided in the Prosecution's motion for the admission of Mr. Januzi's evidence which was filed on the 28th of October, 2008, and of course on Mr. Januzi's written statement which was admitted under Rule 92 quater. And that's as Exhibit P281. Turning next to the second part of question 4(a), the deportation from Suva Reka town between 7 and 21 May 1999. Now, this deportation was pleaded in paragraph 72(d) of the indictment. And the Prosecution submits that, contrary to the Defence argument, 72(d)(i) does not limit the time-frame of Suva Reka, that the indictment must be read as a whole so that the time-frame of the crimes that were committed is January to June 1999. Now, further specificity of this incident was provided, including that the deportations occurred between 7 and 21 May 1999 -- was provided in the 65 ter witness summaries for Halit Berisha and Hysni Berisha. Both of these witnesses also testified at trial in April 2009. Both testified about the deportations from Suva Reka. Turning then to subpart (b) of your question four, forcible transfers from the villages of Brocna and Tusilje. Now, Brocna and Tusilje are villages in Srbica municipality. The attack on this municipality which took place within the indictment period is described in paragraph 72(c) of the indictment. As to Brocna, Djordjevic was provided sufficient notice of this incident in the 65 ter summary of Milazim Thaqi, who also testified about this displacement and was subjected to cross-examination on the subject. I refer Your Honours to T 5005. As to Tusilje, the Prosecution notes that the evidence led at trial shows that Tusilje was a collection point for Kosovo Albanians fleeing from the village of Turicevac and that Djordjevic was convicted of deportations from Turicevac. That's at paragraphs 673 [sic] and 1632 of the indictment [sic]. Therefore, the Chamber need not have entered a conviction relating to this incident. Turning then to the second part of sub(b) which is the forcible transfer from Cuska --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Because I see that the transcript is confused about Tusilje. You're referring to paragraph 73 of the indictment, which subparagraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I see that there's a problem. Let me just clarify, Your Honour, that Djordjevic was convicted of the deportations from Turicevac and that's at trial judgement paragraphs 637 to [sic] 1632.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
