utterances.text: Oh, I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: So my reference was to the trial judgement not to the indictment. So again, the Chamber need not have entered a conviction related to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. That clarifies the matter. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Turning then to Cuska, the forcible transfer in Cuska took place within both the geographic and temporal scope of the indictment. It is within Pec municipality and the attack on this municipality is described in paragraph 72(e). Djordjevic was provided further sufficient notice of this incident in the 65 ter summaries of Hazir Berisha and Tahir Kelmendi. Both witnesses also testified about this incident as did another witness, Fred Abrahams. Berisha and Kelmendi were cross-examined on this issue. Turning then to subpart (c), the murder in the village of Mala Krusa. Now, these murders took place in the course of the attack on Mala Krusa described in paragraph 75(c) of the indictment, as noted by the Trial Chamber at paragraph 485 of the trial judgement. The names of the three men at issue are included in Schedule C to the indictment, those are Sali Shehu, Demir Rashkaj and Nexhat Shehu. Further, on 16 February 2009 Prosecution witness Lutfi Ramadani testified and gave evidence concerning these murders and was cross-examined on the issue. Turning then to the murders in Podujevo town in subpart (c), the murders of Hamdi Duriqi and Selmon Gashi took place in Podujevo on the same day that at least 14 others were murdered as described in paragraph 75(L) of the indictment. While the indictment did not list Duriqi and Gashi by name in the schedule, this was not a material fact that needed to be pled in the indictment. I refer Your Honours to the Kupreskic appeal judgement paragraph 89, and the Naletilic and Martinovic appeal judgement at paragraph 24. In any event, Your Honours, Djordjevic was provided clear and consistent notice regarding these murders. The 65 ter summaries of Fatos Bogojevci and Saranda Bogojevci indicated that these two witnesses would testify that two men were taken into a shop and two gun-shots were heard. Both witnesses testified and they named the two men to be Hamid Duriqi and Selmon Gashi. Finally, turning to the persecutions committed through murder at Pusto Selo, that's in sub(d) of question four. The massacre at Pusto Selo took place in Orahovac municipality on 31 March 1999, and therefore within both the geographic and temporal scope of the indictment. It was also part of the persecutory campaign described in paragraph 16 and -- to 33 of the indictment. Djordjevic was also provided notice of this incident, including its discriminatory nature. In the 65 ter witness list, in summaries of Ali Gjogaj and Beqir Krasniqi. During the trial, Gjogaj and Krasniqi as well as Avdyl Mazreku testified and were cross-examined by the Defence about the crimes in Pusto Selo. The Defence also introduced witnesses and exhibits concerning these crimes. And I refer Your Honours specifically to the testimony of Witness 6D2 on the 3rd of March, 2010, and to Exhibits D225, D226, and D811. To conclude, Your Honours, Djordjevic was provided sufficient notice of each of the incidents noted in question four and he fails in his burden to show that any of the alleged defects to the indictment materially affected his ability to prepare his defence. Now, even if Your Honours do find error here, it should not affect Djordjevic's sentence which, of course, is based on a massive number of crimes committed throughout Kosovo. That concludes my answer to Your Honours' question four. Oh, I'm seeing perhaps a question -- a correction to the transcript again. On page 99, line 6, it should say paragraphs 637, 632, not 637 to 632 -- 1632, sorry. So I meant to say those two paragraphs separately not as a range which, of course, would be an enormous range, not very helpful. Unless there's questions to -- or questions related to my answer to question four, I'd like to take the opportunity to turn to the -- answer the question that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TUZMUKHAMEDOV
utterances.text: Thank you. It is related --

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TUZMUKHAMEDOV
utterances.text: I mean, I have a question that is related.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TUZMUKHAMEDOV
utterances.text: The appellant claims in his brief that he did not receive sufficient notice with regard to events that took place in Dusanovo as the indictment merely accuses Mr. Djordjevic of acts of deportation committed, and then I quote, "in the city of Prizren." However, if you look at the trial judgement, at paragraph 565 it describes Dusanovo as a suburb of Prizren, and then in 1626, Dusanovo is described as neighbourhood of Prizren. And then further the Prosecution exhibit 86 -- 876 describes Dusanovo as the commune of Prizren. What is the correct interpretation to be given to the location of Dusanovo in relation to Prizren? Do you see any conflict between those geographical -- between those geographical descriptions, that is, suburb, neighbourhood, commune? And if you do, how do you reconcile that conflict? And if you do not see any conflict, please explain. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, Tusanovo refers to a suburb of Prizren -- sorry, Dusanovo refers to a suburb of Prizren. Without having before me the specific testimony and 65 ter summaries and so on, I would say that this does provide sufficient notice to the accused, given that it is in close proximity to the town of Prizren and therefore is not necessarily material fact that has to be pled in the indictment. The appellant knew the crime to which he had to answer, he knew that they related to Prizren. The fact that they may have occurred in a town close to Prizren did put him on sufficient notice that that is the crime to which he had to answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TUZMUKHAMEDOV
utterances.text: And if I may, how would you describe the suburb?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it's within Prizren, so in the Prosecution's view, Dusanovo, that would include the geographic community or suburb of Dusanovo, that it is within Prizren. And that would provide him with sufficient notice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TUZMUKHAMEDOV
utterances.text: Okay. So in that sense, both the trial judgement and the exhibit to which I referred where three different terms are used to describe Dusanovo, they should be considered to be equal and the term "the city of Prizren" should embrace them all?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Yes, within Prizren town, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TUZMUKHAMEDOV
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Finally, I wanted to take the opportunity to address Your Honours' question to the Defence, to the appellant, regarding events from 1998. And now Your Honours this morning asked: Can you direct me to anywhere in the trial judgement where the Chamber found it proven beyond a reasonable doubt that a JCE involving General Djordjevic existed prior to January 1999? And if the answer to the first question is negative, then can you direct me to any instances in the trial judgement where the Trial Chamber imposed criminal liability on Djordjevic stemming from events occurring prior to mid-January 1999? The answer to the first question, Your Honours, is no. All of the charged crimes fall within the indictment. And the Trial Chamber made specific findings as to each of the crimes, that they formed part of the joint criminal enterprise. There were no crimes for which Djordjevic was found responsible that did not fall within the JCE period. And in answer to the second part of the question then, contrary to the argument of the appellant, nowhere in the judgement, neither on pages 733 to 781 or elsewhere, does the Chamber impose criminal responsibility on Djordjevic for any contributions that occurred before mid-January of 1999. Rather, the Chamber relied on 1998 conduct and knowledge only to reasonably infer that General Djordjevic shared the intent of the JCE in 1999. And in that vein, Your Honours, the Prosecution agrees with counsel's statement that "knowledge from 1998 could be used, for example, as a means to infer a similar knowledge or intent in the later period." That's at transcript page 61 of today's transcript. Now, this is also consistent with the jurisprudence of this Tribunal, as Your Honours held in the Krajisnik appeal judgement, paragraphs 200 to 204, and at paragraph 492, "the state of mind and conduct of an accused prior to the existence of the common purpose can be taken into consideration as evidence of the accused's JCE mens rea." And that is precisely what the Chamber did in this case. I refer Your Honours to paragraphs 2155 to 2158, which specifically list his contributions. All of these contributions occur in 1999. To conclude, Your Honours, Djordjevic's contributions -- convictions for persecutions, murder, deportation, forcible transfer lie on solid legal and factual foundations. These findings show that Djordjevic was one of the most crucial members of a JCE that unleashed havoc in Kosovo in 1999, inflicting untold suffering on hundreds of thousands Kosovo Albanians who were at the receiving end of the JCE's campaign of terror and extreme violence. In his appeal, Djordjevic has failed to prove that the Chamber's findings are those that no reasonable Chamber could make. His appeal should be dismissed, his conviction upheld, and his sentence increased as requested by the Prosecution in our own appeal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Wood, unless you have got other things to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I noticed earlier on this morning that when you were dealing with the 13th ground of appeal, you suggested towards the end of your submissions on that point that in the event that we consider the Djordjevic ground of appeal in relation to deportation favourably, then we should proceed to enter a conviction for forcible transfer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I understood you at the time either that you were inferring that this flows naturally from the indictment itself or that you were suggesting it as a principle of law that forcible transfer maybe is a minor crime which is subsumed in the whole concept of deportation and forcible movement of people anyway. My question to you is the following: How do you consider a conviction for forcible transfer in relation to the movements to Montenegro as being covered by the indictment? And I am particularly raising this because if you read paragraph 73 of the indictment, with respect to those Kosovo Albanians who were internally displaced, in the words of the indictment itself, within the territory of Kosovo, the Prosecutor re-alleges and incorporates by a reference paragraph 16 to 33, 60 to 64, and 71 and 72 of the indictment. Do you really consider that the indictment also covers forcible transfers to outside the territory of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. First of all, let me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I mean, my question is very simple. How do you argue that short of a finding that there was deportation, we should proceed to convicting for forcible transfer if 73 restricts forcible transfer to displaced within the territory of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: First of all, let me explain, Your Honours, that I hope I didn't give the wrong impression, that the Prosecution considers forcible transfer to be a minor crime that is subsumed within deportation. Of course it's a crime of equal gravity under Article 5(i) of the Statute, and if I gave that impression, then I would want to correct that. Secondly, I would point out that this particular aspect has not been challenged by the Defence. They don't challenge this aspect of the indictment. But lastly, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry, I didn't understand you. Which aspect? Because the Defence --

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: The indictment notice issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, no -- okay. But that's different. Because I never understood the Defence to say that they agree that if there is no deportation, there could be forcible transfer. They never accepted that or conceded that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Well, in paragraph 98 of their reply, Your Honour, they did say, and they repeated it here again today, that if it's anything, it's -- and I'm just -- I'm turning to that page. If it's anything, it's forcible transfer, not deportation. And I read the forced displacement of individuals within a federal state --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But not charged?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Well, again that's not something that's challenged. But to get to the heart of it, Your Honours, the point is that the only difference really between deportation and forcible transfer is the border that's crossed. The Prosecution believes that the indictment has charged -- has put him on sufficient notice that he's responsible for answering for the displacements that occurred in these two municipalities so that the displacement into Montenegro is such a forcible displacement and it can be considered either a forcible transfer or a deportation. And the difference is the question of how Your Honours or how the Trial Chamber has read the indictment -- or, I'm sorry, has analysed the facts. And of course, as the Prosecution has said, they analysed the facts and found that it was a de facto border. Again, he knew the case to which he had to answer, which was the displacements from Kosovska Mitrovica into Pec, so that the displacement across the border is either forcible transfer or deportation. In any event, it's a displacement for which he had to answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Perhaps you would also like to deal with this later on when we resume. We will have a break now. Now, with this understanding, the meeting I have starts at 3.00. I'm told that it's not expected to take as long as one hour, anywhere near that but not as long as one hour. I would suggest that from 20 to 4.00, 20 to 4.00, you are all on stand-by. In case I finish earlier, I will send out messages so that we reconvene as soon as we can so that we will finish earlier than the expected half past 6.00. All right. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. O'Leary, now we come to the reply of the Defence team, 30 minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Thank you again, Your Honour. I'm just going to make a few quick points, only not too quick, on concurrent and cumulative convictions and then I'll hand the floor over to Mr. Hopkins. The Prosecution today has incorrectly stated that Vlastimir Djordjevic was convicted only once in the disposition under each count. On this I will note that you should clearly look at paragraph 2230 of the disposition. The word "and" is critical there. For each count he's found guilty for participation in a joint criminal enterprise and for having aided and abetted the crime of the count. Again, the Prosecution has not shown what specific factors are reflected in the dual conviction that better reflect his conduct. Indeed, it's only a repetition that the two convictions were needed to show his high level of culpability, they've said. My learned colleague has stated that the principle that guided the Trial Chamber was one of totality of conduct as asserted in their response. But we would ask why then not simply make his contribution to the JCE a substantial contribution in the finding at paragraph 2158? As the Prosecutor has pointed out, four types of contribution were taken into account for the JCE and three of the exact same contributing factors made up his aiding and abetting contribution, and that's at today's transcript of T 82. The one that's not considered in aiding and abetting, Your Honours, is one referred to as planning and co-ordination of MUP operations. On this point, Your Honours, we note, one, that Djordjevic was not convicted of planning nor of findings made that he had planned; and two, his role in the MUP is fully reflected in the findings of additional aggravating factors. Since all four were a part of the found JCE contribution, the Trial Chamber, we would say, was free to highlight his culpability under JCE, as the standard set in Brdjanin appeals judgement at paragraph 430, is a significant contribution as the lowest threshold. Today the Prosecutor has focused on Ndindabahizi but we have already addressed that in our brief and in our reply specifically. The citations provided by the Prosecution in Ndindabahizi relate to a proprio motu ground taken by the Appeals Chamber and this was to address convictions of commission and aiding and abetting in the alternative. As in the Gatete appeals judgement, in Ndindabahizi they simply referred to the various modes of liability. They did not separately convict. And what is notable in these paragraphs is the quote that comes from the Trial Chamber -- the appeals judgement that states: "... it is for a Trial Chamber to identify unambiguously the mode(s) of liability for which an accused is convicted and the relation between them." And that's at paragraph 123 of Ndindabahizi. We submit that this was not done in the Djordjevic trial judgement. What's more, Your Honours, we would point out that in that same appeal judgement at paragraph 122 it clearly says, and I quote: "... alternative convictions for several modes of liability are, in general, incompatible with the principle that a judgement has to express unambiguously the scope of the convicted person's criminal responsibility." Judge Guney will recognise this as he agreed with this statement in his partial dissent at paragraph 2. This goes to the core of our submissions, Your Honours, that convictions for JCE and aiding and abetting along with that alternative finding of a JCE III liability are ambiguous. On the point of commission and other forms of liability, I would point further to Judge Guney's dissent on this point, in particular paragraph 4. The Prosecution states that this is a matter of discretion for the Trial Chamber, and that's at transcript 83, but Your Honours, we would submit that this is outside the limits of discretion to convict on these two modes of liability. While the convictions are unambiguous, the relation between them is not. They are based on the exact same findings and this, we submit, is an abuse of discretion. The Prosecution also stated today that: We've shown no prejudice. And that's at transcript 83 and 86. But in fact, Your Honours, we have pointed to prejudice in our brief, again in our reply, and again today. Today I specifically pointed out three errors and I did not have time to fully enunciate the Kunarac et al. appeals judgement statement in regarding that second point of prejudice, but I did point to it at paragraph 169 of the Kunarac appeals judgement and I'll take this opportunity now to quickly read it to you. That: "At the very least, such persons suffer the stigma inherent in being convicted of an additional crime for the same conduct." And "in a more tangible sense, there may be such consequences as losing eligibility for early release under the law of the state enforcing the sentence." Your Honours, it has been stated time and again that cumulative and concurrent convictions should not be made without great care so as to not double punish. And very recently, the honourable President has stated in his dissent in the Gatete appeal judgement, "it is vital to recall," and I am quoting, "as was done in the Popovic et al. case, that the fundamental principle animating the concern regarding multiple convictions for the same act is one of fairness to the accused and that there is a real risk of prejudice which lies in allowing cumulative convictions," and that's in the honourable Judge Agius's dissent in paragraph 6 of the Gatete appeals judgement. Here, Your Honours, the risk of prejudice is realised with the higher sentence to Vlastimir Djordjevic. And I'll hand the floor over if there are no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. O'Leary. Mr. Hopkins -- yes, Judge Guney would like to put a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: Well, Djordjevic submit that duplicate conviction under Article 7(1) for the same crime are impermissible and logically incompatible, so I would like then you make -- you elaborate on this part. The second little question is: The impact, if any, of the reversal of conviction based on aiding and abetting and of Djordjevic's contention that his sentence was increased to the double conviction will be left for consideration at later stage or should we consider it right now? When I say "later stage," it may be other example sentencing stage, for example.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Thank you for your questions, Your Honours. In submitting that they're logically incompatible, it has to do with the nature of the modes of liability, one being a principal and one being an accomplice. And we carefully outlined the distinction in our brief that the jurisprudence has tried to divide joint criminal enterprise from aiding and abetting for the past almost two decades, and specifically point to what actions and what mens rea and actus reus are required for each specific mode of liability, JCE I, JCE III, and aiding and abetting. And we would submit that if you have a finding for all three of them, you are asking the person to have three separate mens reas in his own same mind for the same conduct, which is logically incompatible. You can't aid and abet your own crimes. At the same time, the impact of reversal for aiding and abetting or if either one of these would fall away is simply that his sentence must be reduced. It would be a fallacy for us to think that, at the end of the trial judgement, the Chamber did not look at how many convictions there were and on how many counts and take this into consideration in the totality of factoring his sentence. And we would submit that his sentence was raised based on the fact that there were two convictions for each count and that three of the counts were impermissibly cumulative to the persecutions, Count 5. And have I answered your question fully, Your Honour? Thank you. Barring any further, I'll hand over, Your Honours. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOPKINS
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I will address you on a number of points in the order that I noted them as the Prosecution was speaking, rather than the order I necessarily addressed them when I rose first thing this morning. Firstly, the standard on appeal. The standard on appeal is whether we can point to other reasonable inferences that existed. It is not, as the Prosecution repeatedly suggested, whether it was a reasonable conclusion that Djordjevic shared the intent of the JCE. That's not the test. Rather, our understanding of the law is that what we need to persuade you of is whether other reasonable inferences existed; and if they did, you should intervene. Now, perhaps the relevant test can be put this way: No reasonable Trial Chamber would convict when other reasonable inferences consistent with innocence existed. Now, that was the Appeals Chamber's approach in the Bizimungu and Mugenzi appeal recently and also in the Gotovina appeal recently. So in Mugenzi, did other reasonable inferences exist about his involvement in the decision to remove the Préfet of Butare and his subsequent attendance at the installation ceremony in Butare when President Sindikubwabo made his speech? Yes, they did, hence an acquittal. In Gotovina, did other reasonable inferences exist about the intent behind attacks on towns like Knin and the pattern of crimes? Yes. So the undoubted pattern that there was in that case could not be tied to the leadership. An acquittal followed on appeal. And that was a case where the leader in question had actually said that he could destroy Knin if he wanted to. See paragraphs 93 and 94 of the judgement. Djordjevic on appeal just asks for the same treatment. Now, even if you are of the view that the inferences that the Trial Chamber drew can survive appellate review, we say that the level of Djordjevic's responsibility for events in Kosovo is still demonstrably overstated, his sentence is extreme. And moving on to the next point I've noted about Djordjevic's role in 1998 versus his role in 1999. Now, when you review the judgement as a whole, it is, in our submission, striking how different Djordjevic's role is in relation to the indictment crimes versus the earlier role. And when you look at the judgement as a whole, it's striking the extent to which Djordjevic's liability is based on events that predated the JCE. Now, it's Djordjevic's more limited role in 1999 that led the Trial Chamber in this case, in our submission, to overreach, to hark back to events in the summer of 1998 or the October Agreements, and so on, or even Racak in early 1999, which is not clear, to us anyway, whether that pre-dates or post-dates when the JCE was found to have come into existence. So, in fact, what we say one sees as an accumulation of indicators that, for whatever reason, Djordjevic's role diminished as 1998 wore on and into 1999. Now, we say that this is an approach that no reasonable Trial Chamber would take to ignore that obvious change, particularly when - and this is an important point - when the parties were explicitly told in the trial to focus on the period of the indictment crimes for March 1999 onwards. Now, we heard during the course of the Prosecutor's response this morning a righteous recitation of aspects of the crimes that were committed in Kosovo, for example, racist remarks that were uttered by perpetrators on the ground, like "Serbia, Serbia," as they crossed the boundary, internal boundary, between Kosovo and Montenegro. But, if Djordjevic is to be judged on the basis of those remarks made by the rank-and-file of the MUP or the VJ on the ground in Kosovo in 1999, we would respectfully suggest that many militaries and police forces better prepare for prosecution before international tribunals. Those are things we would suggest are of limited relevance to the key question before you today which is Djordjevic's responsibility. Now, the next question, the next point I noted was, Mr. President, your question on the deportation to Montenegro and you'd asked specifically about paragraph 73 of the indictment, the issue there, does that paragraph include forcible transfer outside of Kosovo. Now, the target of our appeal is the conviction that Djordjevic has, which is a deportation conviction. So we have not developed submissions in our brief about whether this alternative was in the indictment. And all our submissions have intended to do today was, as I think, Mr. President, you noted, to distinguish the two crimes, deportation on the one hand, forcible transfer on the other. Now, we do not say for a moment that Djordjevic should be convicted of forcible transfer in the alternative. The relief sought at paragraph 328 of our appeal brief is explicitly to quash his deportation convictions. Now, perhaps if the indictment had addressed this matter and pleaded population movement from Kosovo to Montenegro as being forcible transfer, this would all have been litigated at trial. And the very nature of your question, I would suggest, and the question that we addressed this morning, to refer to the record, rather shows that the case was just not fought on this basis. Now, perhaps you will develop Stakic in the future in another case, but given the way the indictment was pleaded here, in my submission, this is just not the case for it. Fourthly, Djordjevic 's knowledge and communications with Kosovo during the indictment period, so in 1999. The Prosecution this morning placed particular emphasis on the finding in the trial judgement that Djordjevic was notified in oral reports during the indictment period. The submission made was that this showed him continuing his involvement with Kosovo during the indictment period. Now, we say again - and we said this this morning - that the trial judgement warps its own findings. You see a metamorphosis about - and this is another example - the reporting system in the MUP. So at paragraph 1986 of the judgement you see a -- what looks like a damning conclusion that the SUPs in Kosovo reported to Belgrade by telephone and that daily reports, so on, were sent as well. Now, as I say, this conclusion involved a metamorphosis because the original finding earlier in the judgement at paragraph 130 is that communication -- the communications system, excuse me, between Kosovo and Belgrade was cut, damaged by the NATO bombing, by early April. You see that the SUPs could call Pristina, but crucially not Belgrade. And you see that when you look to the evidence that the Trial Chamber cites in that paragraph, 130, which was the evidence of Cvetic, a Prosecution witness, at transcript 6723. So in our submission, the later finding, the metamorphosis, at paragraph 1986 of the judgement is just misleading. The next point I'd noted was the decision to incorporate the Skorpions and whether any innocent inferences remained following that decision. Now, at about 8.20 at night on the 24th of March, 1999, NATO forces unleashed a ferocious attack on the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. The stated reason was that Yugoslav forces had themselves unleashed a ferocious attack against Kosovo Albanian civilians, but the trial judgement in this case rather undermines NATO's narrative of an extant attack on the civilian population at that stage. Indeed, the indictment doesn't charge crimes that pre-dated NATO's attack. And so the trial judgement repeatedly draws an inference that military action by FRY forces was disproportionate to the threat faced. But nowhere, and this is a point we make in our brief, do you see a global assessment of the threat that the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia faced. And on the actual decision to incorporate the Skorpions into the MUP, our respectful submission on appeal is that, yes, this happened and you will not think it an attractive decision. But in the circumstances, it was not necessarily criminal. For example, surely it's better that the Skorpions were incorporated into the MUP, that it was sought to control them, give them police uniforms as we were told this morning, badges, rather than just send them in to Kosovo. Now, the Prosecution rightly said that Djordjevic was not convicted of crimes after the -- for crimes that the Skorpions committed after they were redeployed, but that is our point. His liability was based nevertheless, at least on part, on what happened after they'd been redeployed. If this was an element of the conduct, Djordjevic's conduct, upon which the Prosecution wanted to rely for a conviction, why wasn't this charged? On Stevanovic and Zekovic I only have, I think, two or perhaps three more points to cover, there was simply no evidence that they were the heads of administrations within the RJB as opposed to being assistant ministers. The Prosecution this morning relied on the Trial Chamber's finding of that, but our submission is that the finding is just not based on any evidence. Indeed, it's notable that the Prosecution this morning didn't point to any evidence of this, and we would suggest the conclusion is bizarre. And still on Stevanovic and Zekovic, we say that the trial judgement suffers from a fundamental error because it did not follow the Appeals Chamber's judgement in Krajisnik by identifying the specific role played by JCE members and making specific findings how those JCE members used principal perpetrators to commit the crimes. Now, contrast that approach in Krajisnik, in particular paragraphs 283 to 284 of that judgement, contrast that with what's happened in Djordjevic's case. Now, we have JCE members identified in a list at paragraph 2127 of the judgement, but we don't know what their role was, how they actually were said to have used principal perpetrators to -- and so it's this, in our submission, that causes us to struggle to explain - if we are struggling to explain - exactly what the role and the overlaps were between Stevanovic's role as assistant minister on the one hand and his role in the RJB, if any, on the other. A brief point on aiding and abetting and the issue of whether or not Djordjevic was a remote aider and abettor or a proximate, I think was the word used, aider and abettor. Now, in the run-up to the NATO bombing, you see a number of dispatches whereby Djordjevic either signs or somebody else signs on his behalf, sending units to Kosovo. But given that a major war was imminent, we say that there is nothing obviously criminal in that, nor is it inconsistent with his figurehead role in the RJB. And Djordjevic lost out of scrutiny of those types of issues by not looking at them through a specific direction lens. The trial judgement and the OTP this morning says that when crimes were committed in Kosovo, Djordjevic travelled there on a number of occasions, twice I think. But -- and they were using that -- those examples to buttress their submission that he was a proximate aider and abettor rather than a remote one. But if you look at the chronology of the crime base, what you will see was that the closest crime to Djordjevic's visits to Kosovo on the 16th and 18th of April was Kladernica, which we have an issue about whether or not it was in the indictment, and Urosevac train station on the 15th of April. There is a suggestion that crimes were committed in Srbica, in Prizren municipality, from the 9th to the 16th of April, perhaps. We just don't know whether that overlapped with Djordjevic's visit at all. But it's just -- it's not apparent to us how it is said that Djordjevic would have known about those when he travelled to Pristina. A brief point, this is my penultimate point, on rank in the hierarchy of the MUP. The MUP did not work, as the Prosecutor sought to say this morning, as a strict hierarchy. A good example of this is that Branko Djuric was the chief of the Belgrade SUP for a while. He was a lieutenant-colonel. His assistant, so his subordinate, was Sreten Lukic, who was a major-general. Now, we can see those ranks in Exhibits D400 and D423. So the point is that Djuric was Lukic's boss until Lukic was sent to Kosovo in the summer of 1998, but he had an inferior rank. And that a lieutenant-colonel is junior to a major-general you can see in Exhibit P49. My last point that I had noted was the point about whether or not crime sites were in the indictment, question four that you had posed to us this morning. Now, the prejudicial effect of a defective indictment can be remedied, we don't dispute that, but only if the Prosecution provides an accused with clear, timely, and consistent information that resolves ambiguity or clarifies vagueness. But the jurisprudence, in particular, the Simic appeal judgement paragraph 23, emphasises that there can only be a limited number of cases that fall into that category. Now, it is right, as the Prosecution said, to say that where an appellant raises a defect in the indictment for the first time on appeal, he bears the burden of proving that his ability to prepare his defence is materially impaired. But that principle is just of no application in this case. This isn't a vague indictment capable of being cured; it's a very, very specific indictment. Djordjevic could only know that these additional convictions would be entered when the trial judgement was handed down, and if that's not prejudice, I don't know what is. Now, frankly, if the Prosecution wanted to spend its time, its trial time, leading evidence of uncharged events, then that's a matter for the Prosecution. Another point arises on this. The logic of the Prosecution's submission would seem to be that Djordjevic should also have been convicted for everything that happened in 1998, but the indictment just wasn't pleaded on that basis. So in conclusion --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, because your time is up.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOPKINS
utterances.text: -- Djordjevic didn't plan, instigate, or order a single crime in Kosovo. You see that finding at paragraph 2167 and 2168 of the judgement. In particular, there's no nexus, it's said, between anything Djordjevic did and the crimes. It is our submission on appeal that the evidence in this case viewed as a whole shows the concentration of power away from Djordjevic to Kosovo itself to reflect the threat there. It's far too simplistic to say that he was the number two man in the ministry and therefore is responsible for everything that happened. The Trial Chamber got the ministry wrong and it got Djordjevic wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we move on to the Prosecution appeal. You have 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: In my submissions today, I will address the Prosecution's first ground of appeal and also respond to Your Honours' question number six relating to the Trial Chamber's treatment of persecution based on sexual assaults. We will not be making submissions on ground two of our appeal. This ground concerns the manifestly inadequate sentence imposed on the accused and has been fully briefed in our written submissions. Turning to our submissions on ground one. Your Honours, at the heart of our appeal on ground one lies a simple proposition, that the crime of sexual assault should not be treated differently from other violent acts simply because of its sexual component. And this is what the Chamber did in this case. The outcome of this case as it stands means that more specific evidence of discriminatory intent is required to prove sexual assault as an underlying act of persecution than for other violent acts. As a result of this error, the Chamber found that persecution through sexual assault had not been established in this case and it did not go on to deal with the question of whether Djordjevic was responsible for these crimes. My submissions today therefore cover two issues which also respond to the two issues in question six that Your Honours have posed. First, I will deal with the discriminatory intent underlying the Beleg and Pristina sexual assaults. I will explain why, given the context surrounding these incidents, the only reasonable conclusion is that they were committed with discriminatory intent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Judge Guney has a question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: Well, assuming that the Appeals Chamber finds in favour of establishing persecution through sexual assault, can you elaborate on the prevalence of sexual assaults in Kosovo during 1998 and 1999 in order to assist the Appeals Chamber in determining whether or not sexual assaults were a natural and foreseeable consequence of the JCE. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: There's several parts to Your Honour's question and I will deal with them in turn as I proceed with my submissions, but if I can just respond briefly now, Your Honour. Our position is that we do not need to establish that sexual assault was, in fact, prevalent during the conflict in order for -- to prove that persecutions through sexual assault was established, that the requirement of discriminatory intent required for persecution through sexual assault was established. And our position is also that we do not need to establish that sexual assault was prevalent in order for this crime to have been foreseeable to General Djordjevic. And I will get to this in the course of my submissions and elaborate further upon this issue, Your Honour. So I will be addressing this when I deal both with the issue of discriminatory intent and also foreseeability. If that's okay, I will explain our position further as I proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that is okay with you, Judge Guney. Thank you. Let's proceed then. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I was speaking about the first issue that I will address which is the issue of discriminatory intent, and in doing so, I will also deal with the sexual assaults in Pristina and Beleg were not established or the Chamber found had not been established and explain why these too amounted to persecution. And second, I will explain how the Trial Chamber's findings and evidentiary record show beyond reasonable doubt that persecution based on sexual assault was foreseeable to the JCE members including Djordjevic. And we ask Your Honours to correct the Trial Chamber's errors, find that the Beleg and Pristina sexual assaults constitute persecution, and enter convictions pursuant to JCE III for Djordjevic. Turning to the five incidents of sexual violence at issue in this appeal and to the first part of Your Honours' question of whether the element of discriminatory intent for persecution is satisfied in relation to this incident, and if we could please have the slide be brought up in Sanction. The Trial Chamber accepted that the rapes of two women -- thank you. The Trial Chamber accepted that the rapes of two women, K20 in Beleg village and K14 in Pristina, were proved but stated that the Prosecution brought "no specific evidence" from which it could infer that the rapes were carried out with a discriminatory intent required for persecution, paragraph 1796. Concerning the three other victims that are listed up on the slide, the two Kosovo Albanian sisters in Beleg village and the Kosovo Albanian girl in a convoy in Pristina municipality, the Chamber found that the allegations of sexual assault were not proven, paragraphs 1792 and 1794. In relation to the two proven incidents, the Chamber ignored direct evidence of discriminatory intent and failed to consider any of the general or specific contextual factors surrounding the sexual assault incidents. These factors are highly relevant in assessing discriminatory intent on the facts on this case and as confirmed by the Appeals Chamber in the Krnojelac case. And that is the Krnojelac appeal judgement paragraphs 184 and 188. In relation to the three sexual assaults that the Chamber found were not established, the Chamber wrongly found that circumstantial evidence was insufficient to establish these crimes and reached an unreasonable conclusion on the basis of the evidence. Had the Chamber properly considered and analysed all relevant evidence, it would have found that Serb forces targeted and persecuted all five women and girls in Beleg and Pristina because they were Kosovo Albanian. And this is illustrated by the context surrounding the sexual assaults. And we can remove the slide. Turning first to the sexual assaults in Beleg village, we have set out the details in paragraphs 25 through 39 of our appeal brief, and I will only highlight some key points here today. K20 and the two young Kosovo Albanian sisters were sexually assaulted during the Serb campaign to drive Kosovo Albanians out of Beleg. In late March 1999, Serb forces attacked the village of Beleg. During the course of this attack, Serb forces expelled K20 and her family from their home. The family was then held in a basement in the village along with hundreds of other villagers. That night, K20 was taken from the basement with two other Kosovo Albanian girls, who were sisters, to a burned-out house. There four Serb soldiers gang-raped her. A Serb policeman, this same policeman who had expelled K20's family from their home that same morning, stood guard while the soldiers took turns raping her. While K20 was being raped, she could hear the two sisters screaming. When she was finally released, this policeman told her: "The UCK," referring to the Kosovo Liberation Army, "did worse than they're doing. You can handle them." This remark which the Chamber ignored shows that K20 was targeted because of her ethnicity. The next day the entire village of Beleg was expelled and ordered to head to Albania by Serb forces. Now, in relation to all three incidents, the Chamber failed to consider the context that all the women and girls held in the basement were Kosovo Albanians who had been expelled from their homes and who Serb forces aimed to drive out of Kosovo through violence. In relation to K20, the Chamber failed to consider the Serb policeman's remark as direct evidence of discriminatory intent, just as it had considered similar remarks as supporting discriminatory intent against Kosovo Albanians when assessing other forms of persecution: Murder and forcible transfer, for example, in paragraphs 618, 720, 824, 1192, and more generally paragraphs 1777, and 1783 to 1789. In relation to the two Kosovo Albanian sisters, the Chamber erred in failing to consider the totality of the evidence in assessing whether these sisters had been sexually assaulted --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I know you have referred to the paragraphs, but could you just summarise what is in those paragraphs briefly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: In those paragraphs that I've referred to, there are references -- there are recitations of evidence by the Trial Chamber where they quote to different statements made by perpetrators either during the forcible expulsions or during the murders, and generally there are statements such as: Where is the KLA? Why aren't they here to save you? Where is NATO? And similar statements of that sort --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And your point is that that is corresponding evidence indicating a discriminatory intent?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Well, the Chamber itself took it into account as evidence of discriminatory intent. In fact, at paragraph 1777 and also 1783 to 1789, when they deal with the forcible expulsions and the murders, they specifically refer to the fact that the perpetrators as they are committing these crimes made remarks to the victims which showed that they were targeting them because of their ethnicity and they were making derogatory remarks in the process of committing these crimes. So what we're saying is that the statement made to K20 is similar to other remarks the Chamber did take into account when assessing other crimes. Thank you. In relation to the two Kosovo Albanian sisters, the Chamber erred in failing to consider the totality of the evidence in assessing whether the sisters had been sexually assaulted. It ignored K20's evidence that she overheard the sisters screaming at the same locality or location where she was being raped and it failed to draw the only reasonable inference from K58's corroborating evidence that the girls were crying when they returned to the basement. The only reasonable inference on the totality of this evidence is that these three victims were sexually assaulted because they were Kosovo Albanian. They were evicted from their homes, imprisoned in inhumane conditions, sexually assaulted, and finally expelled from Kosovo, fulfilling the aims of the JCE to persecute and forcibly expel the Kosovo Albanian population. To separate the acts of sexual violence from the other persecutory acts the victims endured as the Chamber did is simply wrong. Now, turning to the Pristina sexual assaults, these crimes and the Trial Chamber's errors in assessing them bear similar hallmarks to those in Beleg, and we have set out the details in paragraphs 8 to 24 of our appeal brief and I will not go through the details again here. But both of the victims in Pristina, K14 and the girl in the convoy, were sexually assaulted during the Serb expulsion campaign in that municipality. As the facts relating to K14 show, like the victims in Beleg, Serb forces targeted K14 for expulsion and rape because she was a Kosovo Albanian woman. In fact, only a few days later after being raped, fearing further rapes, she and her family fled to Macedonia. In relation to the girl in the convoy, she too was targeted because she was a Kosovo Albanian. The Chamber failed to consider the girl's sexual assault in the context of the persecutory campaign by Serb forces to drive the Kosovo Albanian population from Kosovo. The young girl was, in fact, in a convoy fleeing with hundreds of other Kosovo Albanian refugees and Serb forces directed this convoy and terrorised the refugees on the road. Now, the Chamber found that the Serb attacks on Beleg and Pristina were undoubtedly part of the broader attack on the Kosovo Albanian population, paragraph 1597. And the Chamber also found that the deportations in Pristina and Beleg were acts of persecution, paragraphs 1701, 1774, and 1777. And in doing so, the Chamber inferred discriminatory intent from the fact that the overwhelming majority of those forcibly displaced were Kosovo Albanian, which indicated that they were targeted specifically, paragraph 1777. And the Chamber followed a similar reasoning for the murders, paragraph 1781, and for cultural destruction, paragraph 1855. Your Honours, if Serb forces attacking and cleansing Beleg and Pristina were acting with discriminatory intent when they imprisoned, deported, murdered Kosovo Albanians and damaged Kosovo Albanian property, how could they suddenly not be acting with discriminatory intent when they raped or otherwise abused the five Kosovo Albanian women and girls as part of the same conduct? Turning to the question asked by Your Honour Judge Guney, the Chamber took a different approach when assessing the sexual assaults based on the number of incidents, and that's at paragraph 1796. Our submission, which is what I was stating earlier, is that this approach is legally wrong. There is no legal requirement that a certain numeric threshold of sexual assaults be proven in order for these acts to amount to persecution. And the Appeals Chamber has, in fact, confirmed this numerous times, that a single act may be sufficient. For example, in the Kordic appeal judgement, paragraph 102; and Blaskic appeal judgement, paragraph 135. And more generally, the Appeals Chamber has also confirmed that a single act of rape can qualify as a crime against humanity, for example, in the Kunarac appeal judgement, paragraphs 96 and 97. Even if the perpetrator's motivation was entirely sexual, it does not follow that the perpetrators did not act with discriminatory intent, as the Appeals Chamber has, in fact, confirmed in the Kunarac case, appeal judgement, paragraphs 153 and 155. There is no reasonable basis for concluding that the Beleg and Pristina sexual assaults were not carried out with discriminatory intent and we ask you to confirm that they amounted to persecution. Turning to the second limb of my argument and also to the second part of Your Honours' question of whether all the required elements of JCE III liability are met in this case, persecution based on sexual assault was foreseeable to the JCE members, including Djordjevic. The Chamber found that Djordjevic shared the intent to participate in a common plan to modify Kosovo's demographic balance by a campaign of violence and terror against Kosovo Albanian civilians, paragraph 2158. And it found that persecutions, through deportation, forcible transfer, murder, and destruction of cultural property, was part of this common criminal plan, paragraphs 2149 and also 2151. If persecution through murder was part of the common objective, then other violations of physical integrity, such as persecution through sexual violence, were at the very least foreseeable, particularly in light of the fact that the common objective was to be achieved through a campaign of violence and terror. Your Honours, foreseeability for the purposes of JCE III must be assessed with reference to the overall context in which the crimes were committed and particularly in light of the nature of the common criminal purpose. While evidence that the accused knew that the same types of crimes had been previously committed might be a relevant contextual factor, it is not the only one and it is certainly not an essential ingredient in proving foreseeability. Many cases at the Tribunal have adopted this approach. The Krstic case is a clear example of this. For reference, Krstic trial judgement paragraphs 616 and 617; in Krstic appeal judgement, paragraph 149. The Kvocka case is another example, and we've dealt with this case in more detail in our reply brief, paragraphs 16 and 17. Your Honours, if you carry out a similar contextual analysis in this case, the only reasonable conclusion is that Djordjevic could foresee that sexual assault persecutions might happen. Turning to Djordjevic's knowledge, the Chamber found that Djordjevic had detailed knowledge of the events on the ground in Kosovo in 1998 and in 1999, paragraphs 1985 to 1998. Specifically, Djordjevic was well aware of the prevailing contextual factors which made sexual assault persecutions foreseeable in this case. He knew that the forcible expulsion campaign would be implemented by Serb forces through violence and terror, paragraphs 2126, 2129, 2130. He knew that Kosovo Albanian women and girls would be placed in circumstances rendering them especially vulnerable. In fact, the whole point of the criminal plan he endorsed was to force the Kosovo Albanian population, including the women and the girls, from the safety and the security of their homes, paragraphs 2126 and 2129. More significantly, Your Honours, as my colleague Mr. Wood already explained, from the outset of the campaign, Djordjevic knew that forces under his command were directly targeting vulnerable women and children. His knowledge of the massacre of 14 women and children in Podujevo by the Skorpions on 28th March 1999, only four days after this campaign began, is a concrete example of this, paragraph 1993. And finally, he put no meaningful safe-guards in place to prevent crimes from happening; to the contrary, he established a pervasive culture of impunity among his subordinates by failing to punish and by actively concealing their crimes. For reference paragraphs 1966, 1981, 1985, 1994, and 1999. ICTY case law confirms the relevance of -- oh.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I have a question but I want to revert to the question of the evidence needed for discriminatory intent.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: No problem, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If you'd rather finish, I could ask it at the end.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I have only a couple more minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: It's up to Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, conclude and then I'll ask it at the end.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. I was referring to ICTY case law which confirms the relevance of the factors that I have just set out in predicting sexual violence and/or other violent crimes. And for example, I refer Your Honours to the Krstic trial judgement, paragraph 616, and appeal judgement, paragraph 149; Kvocka trial judgement, paragraph 327; Stakic appeal judgement, paragraphs 93 and 95; and Stanisic and Zupljanin trial judgement, volume II, paragraphs 525, 526, and 776. From the factors I have referred to, Your Honours should take the violent nature of the common purpose into account as a very significant predictive factor. In its judgement, the Trial Chamber repeatedly confirmed that the use of violence and terror was an essential component of the common purpose. For example, in paragraphs 2035, 2126, and 2129. It is obvious that in order to permanently uproot hundreds of thousands of Kosovo Albanians, the armed Serb forces had to use violence, including door-to-door expulsions, to terrify the targeted population into leaving. And it is also obvious that in implementing this campaign, these forces would come into one-to-one physical contact with the population and that violent crimes against civilians, including against women and girls, might happen. And this is exactly what the Chamber found when dealing with the crime of murder. The Chamber made alternative findings that murder was a JCE III crime, paragraph 2153. And in finding that murder was foreseeable to Djordjevic, the Chamber indicated that it had no doubt that JCE members were aware of the possibility that Kosovo Albanian women and children might be killed by Serb forces in the course of implementing orders to enter towns and villages and clear them of Kosovo Albanians, paragraphs 2139, 2141, and 2145. If the overarching use of violence and terror in carrying out the expulsion campaign is relevant in predicting violations of physical integrity like persecution through murder, then it is equally relevant in predicting violations of physical integrity like persecution through sexual assault. Not only was the possibility of persecutory sexual assault foreseeable to Djordjevic, he willingly took the risk that this would happen by joining and continuing to participate in that enterprise, paragraph 2158. And since we have a few minutes left, I can address Your Honour's question before my time is up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, as I said, I wanted to revert to the question of the evidence needed for discriminatory intent to establish persecutions. It would be correct to say, wouldn't it, that for the most part this is going to be by inference? You may have direct evidence, but for the most part I think it would be a matter of inference; and if that is so, it would be governed by the principle that that inference should be the only reasonable inference, there should be no other possibility of another reasonable inference. Now, I find this the most interesting but, at the same time, the most difficult aspect of this entire appeal. Very, very difficult for me to know which way to go so I need all the help that I can get from both parties. Would it be reasonable to explain the sexual assault on the basis that it was just done for sexual gratification? Would that not be another reasonable inference?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I briefly touched upon that issue and I can go back to it, but this Appeals Chamber has made clear that we should not confuse motive and intent. And regardless of whether the perpetrators of these crimes were acting due to -- because they were looking for sexual gratification or because they were simply taking advantage of the circumstances, that does not preclude a finding that they were, in fact, acting with discriminatory intent. And what we're asking Your Honours to do is to look at the context -- the circumstances surrounding these crimes in order to establish that they were, in fact, committed with discriminatory intent, and this is why I've drawn the parallel with the other crimes that the Chamber found had been established as persecutions or as underlying acts of persecutions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Might have been wrong in that finding. I'm just making the comment. You're referring to the Chamber making other findings, but that assumes that we will agree or that I will agree that the Chamber was correct in those findings.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I understand your point, Your Honour, but we should not forget that at the core of this entire campaign of violence and terror that the Chamber found had been established in its judgement was the crime of persecution against the Kosovo Albanian population which the Chamber found had been committed through a series of underlying acts, murder, deportations, forcible transfer, and cultural destruction. This clearly shows that the JCE members, including Djordjevic, intended to discriminate against Kosovo Albanians. So the point I was making earlier is if this is at the core of this campaign, the intention to discriminate against the Kosovo Albanian population, and if the perpetrators of these crimes on the ground were found to be acting with discriminatory intent when they expelled the population, for example, in Beleg, from their homes and then they imprisoned them and then they sexually assault the women, they beat the men, and the next day deport everyone, if they are found to be acting with discriminatory intent when they are carrying out all these other acts, we cannot artificially separate the acts of sexual violence the victims endured from all the other forms of violence that they endured which were found to be persecutory acts. And this is why we are asking Your Honours to look at the crimes committed in the context that they were committed, and this is an error we have pointed out in the way the Chamber approached these crimes. The Chamber clearly separated them out from all the other forms of violence that it found had amounted to persecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Have you precedence from our case law in which Trial Chambers or the Appeals Chamber has erred in similar circumstances? Such evidence to be good evidence of discriminatory intent.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Well, the case law I have referred to is -- and I don't know how I'm doing with time, but the case law I had referred to is the Krnojelac appeal judgement, paragraph 184 to 188, where the Appeals Chamber confirmed that the fact that something happens at the same time of the broader discriminatory attack does not mean that an inference of discrimination can automatically be drawn. But the Appeals Chamber also confirmed that if the circumstances surrounding the commission of the specific crimes are consistent with the broader discriminatory attack, which in this case the Chamber found to be established, then of course discriminatory intent may be inferred from contextual factors. And this is what we are asking Your Honours to do to apply that. And I had -- as I had indicated, the Chamber in this case, in fact, found for both Beleg and Pristina that the crime of persecutions had been established in this -- as an underlying act, it found that deportation had been established as a crime of persecution. And I've referred to the specific paragraph where that finding has been made. So they have made a general finding that this attack was part of a broader attack on the Kosovo Albanian population and that the crime of persecutions in these localities had been established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. At the end of the day, the bottom line is what Judge Robinson pointed out, namely, that this being a matter of inference, whether what you are suggesting basically is the only reasonable inference that a reasonable trier of fact can reach. Okay. So we'll have a break now which -- until 5.30, so instead of 30 minutes, 25 minutes. Okay. And we will resume after that, 5.30 sharp, with your response. And from there we'll proceed towards concluding this hearing. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. O'Leary, you have 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And good afternoon again to Your Honours and thank you for the opportunity to respond to the Prosecution. We feel we have put our most salient points in our written response and we will try not to reiterate them here. The Prosecution has raised some points today that I will respond to, but I'll frame them in the context of your sixth question relating to the Prosecution's first ground of appeal. The question you've asked us is: Was the element of discriminatory intent for persecutions satisfied with regard to the rapes of witnesses K14 and K20 as well as the alleged sexual assaults of the girl in the convoy and the two young Kosovo Albanian women in Beleg? There is one answer to all of those incidents, Your Honours, and it's no. The Trial Chamber did not find discriminatory intent as the evidence was not there to establish a dolus specialis. This is important to remember, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. If someone could assist, the headphones of Judge Guney seem to have gone bust. Okay, Ms. O'Leary.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Thank you. It's important to note that the Prosecution charged these sexual assaults not as their own crimes against humanity but as underlying acts of persecution, knowing that the element of discrimination against a protected group must be proven beyond a reasonable doubt. Noting this, the Trial Chamber held at paragraph 1796 that this required the Prosecution to prove that the perpetrators acted with intent to discriminate against the ethnic Kosovo Albanians as an ethnic group. The Trial Chamber found two incidents of sexual assault but found that, and I quote: "No specific evidence has been presented with respect to either of these incidents, that the perpetrators acted with an intent to discriminate." Citing to the limited number of incidents, the Trial Chamber properly found that, and I quote: "The ethnicity of the two victims alone is not a sufficient basis to establish that the perpetrators acted with a discriminatory intent." And, Your Honours, we're talking about two incidents here. The Prosecution has mentioned five incidents because they are putting together the three that were not found. Evidence simply was not sufficient to make a finding beyond a reasonable doubt that there was sexual assault against these unknown women, much less the intent of the perpetrators. It was not the only reasonable inference. If we look to the law cited by the Trial Chamber as setting forth the standard it employed in assessing the evidence of discrimination in the cases of K14 and K20, it is important to note that it is not sufficient for an accused to be aware that he or she is, in fact, acting in any way that's discriminatory. He or she must consciously intend to discriminate. And that's the Djordjevic trial judgement at paragraph 1759, citing the Brdjanin trial judgement at paragraph 996, and the Kordic and Cerkez trial judgement at paragraph 217. Here it is evident that the Trial Chamber did take the entirety of circumstances of each crime into consideration, and this is shown in the Trial Chamber's ability to establish other persecutory acts based on the context of the circumstances of the exact crimes, notably wanton destruction. I note that the Prosecution has mentioned some of these incidents today that were found in the trial judgement, in particular findings of persecution in killings and wanton destruction, and it's important to read those paragraphs of the trial judgement because in those cases, quite often there is a specific religious connotation that is taking part. That element of it is what lent the Trial Chamber to determine that these were discriminatory acts. Although this should be noted with the fact that the Defence is challenging the far-reaching inferences to establish wanton destruction in our appeal brief at ground 15. With the crime of persecution it is the subjective intent of the perpetrators that matters. The subjective intent was not established on the evidence for these two sexual assaults. We have no idea if, in fact, their motives were discriminatory, and to ask the Appeals Chamber to step in now and say that discriminatory intent is the only reasonable conclusion and reverse the Trial Chamber's considered decision on this point would be a step too far. The evidence of discriminatory intent is simply not established so as to preclude that the direct perpetrators could have been acting with a mere criminal intent, not with specific discriminatory intent. And as stated by the Martic trial judgement at paragraph 473, and I quote: "Not every grave crime in war amounts to a persecutory act." However, we take the Prosecution's definition of applying discrimination from context. Any crime committed by any member of the Serb forces, and this includes basically anyone dressed in a uniform, in Kosovo in 1998 or 1999 would be discriminatory. This is simply untenable. Such a standard would require no evidence beyond the finding of sexual assault. It wouldn't even require a specific defendant because, by this standard, every single police person, every military personnel, in fact every politician would be responsible for a crime of persecution for any sexual assault in Kosovo at this time. This standard is amazingly broad and it violates the principles of a fair trial. Further, this goes against the Appeals Chamber who has specifically held that discriminatory intent may not be inferred directly from the general discriminatory nature of an attack on a civilian population. And this is the jurisprudence that's been cited to, it arises out of several appeals judgements, and it was cited to by the Djordjevic trial judgement at paragraph 1760. The Trial Chamber also referred to the standard that allows inference of discriminatory intent from context, yet they did not find discriminatory intent in this case for these acts. It simply was not the only reasonable conclusion from the evidence. And to answer the latter part of your question, were all of the requisite elements for liability under the third category of joint criminal enterprise met? Again, no. Even if by some stretch discriminatory intent had been found beyond any reasonable doubt for one or all of these incidents, it still does not rise to a level of culpability for Vlastimir Djordjevic. Are sexual assaults foreseeable in every war, even in peace time? And is it foreseeable that there are rapes happening in conflicts that go on even today? Absolutely, we read about it every day. But it does not make it okay and it does not sanction such behaviour. But to say that it is foreseeable in the general context of war criminalises war. It's criminalising the use of any police or military in any situation anywhere in the world. Now, the Prosecution today has cited to some cases and in their brief, in particular the Krstic case, for findings of foreseeability, and they specifically cited to paragraphs 616 and 617, and they are clearly distinguishable from the case at hand, Your Honours. The Krstic case is a Srebrenica case, which I'm sure you're all familiar with, and the specifics of the Krstic case with this foreseeability were focusing on a mass influx of up to 30.000 people, largely women, children, and elderly, who had congregated in a small area over the course of a couple days. Furthermore, it was Krstic's role in being on the ground and witnessing this that gave rise to a foreseeability to Krstic himself based on his communications and proximity to the events and this is very narrow. Similarly, Your Honours, the Prosecution cites to several camps cases where there were detention centres that were being run, in particular today they mention the Stakic case, Kvocka case, and Stanisic and Zupljanin. These are also extremely distinguishable. The facts of these cases, if you're looking to the exact context that was considered by the Chamber, in particular looking at the Kvocka trial judgement at paragraph 327 that was cited today, there they found at the Omarska camp where approximately 36 women were held in detention, it was specifically known to these people that these women were "guarded with men by weapons," and I'm quoting, "who were often drunk, violent, and physically and mentally abusive and who were allowed to act with virtual impunity." Another camps case that gets cited for this foreseeability is the Krnojelac appeal judgement. However, if you look to the facts of that specific case and those actors, we're looking at a camps case again where people are in detention. And in the Krnojelac appeal judgement they're specifically considering two separate groups in the detention centre, Serbs and non-Serbs, who were kept in different conditions with the Serbs being treated in a much better way than the non-Serbs. It was a clearly discriminatory line that was drawn there. Your Honour, in this case we cannot lose sight of the context of the situation. We're talking about the entirety of a police and military force engaged in an entire province over the course of months or even years. It is not limited, as the camps cases, or the Krstic case. And as stated in our response, there are a series of errors that must be found to get to the point of JCE III liability for these crimes for Vlastimir Djordjevic. Leaving aside the fact that the three sexual assaults were not even found that have been discussed today, if we're going even with those two sexual assaults that were found, one, you would need to make a finding of persecutory intent for these two sexual assaults, a finding beyond a reasonable doubt; two, a finding that these sexual assaults were a natural and foreseeable consequence to Vlastimir Djordjevic specifically; and finally, that he willingly took this risk in contributing to the JCE. And what's critical here is number two, Your Honours, the foreseeability must be to that person. There is absolutely no evidence in this case that Vlastimir Djordjevic or even any of his subordinates were aware of these crimes. The two victims who came to testify here clearly testified they did not report the crimes to the local police at any time. And this is for K20 at transcript 8514; and for K14, it's at transcript 9042 to 9043. We have to remember that this is 1999 and the ICTY is up and running and statements are being taken by investigators, and when asked, K20 was asked if she believed that giving her statement to the ICTY was the proper route for investigation and follow-up of the crime, she responded: Yes, of course that's what I thought." There was simply no way to know that these crimes were ongoing. The Prosecution also cites today to Podujevo or concealment as evidence of these crimes, especially given the vulnerability of the women and children that they cite in Podujevo. But, Your Honour, there were not sexual assaults in Podujevo. It is simply a way of referring again to these same crimes of concealment, lack of investigation, and the Skorpions generally to find culpability for Vlastimir Djordjevic. There's simply no evidence of notice to Djordjevic that this type of crime was happening or could happen, and the fact that these two incidents are far from sexual assaults as being part of a widespread campaign or expulsions or even a foreseeable consequence. The intent of Djordjevic is not established -- did not establish a persecutory intent beyond reasonable doubt, and there's nothing in the evidence that shows that he possessed such an intent or that even such an inference can be drawn. And, Your Honours, I have one final point. It must be said that if we are grappling with the issue now, if these findings were made, that is the definition of reasonable doubt and it must go to Vlastimir Djordjevic's favour as the defendant. The Prosecution has to prove their case and they simply have not. They've made no showing that no reasonable Trial Chamber could have come to a conclusion regarding the sexual assaults, and we therefore ask that ground one be rejected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. O'Leary. So I suppose that concludes the Defence response. Prosecution, you have, what, 15 minutes for your reply.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. My colleague in her submissions referred to the fact that it is necessary in order to prove discriminatory intent to establish that the accused must have consciously intended to discriminate. Your Honours, this is a clear finding that the Chamber made in this case. The Chamber found that the crime of persecutions was part of the common criminal purpose in this case, persecutions against the Kosovo Albanian population. And it also found that Djordjevic was a JCE member and that he intended to carry out this common criminal plan, and this is in 2158. So it is clear from these findings that he shared this intent to persecute the Kosovo Albanian population. As for the context that my colleague referred to, when we referred to the circumstances surrounding the incidents we're not speaking about the entirety of the conflict. We're referring to the specific circumstances surrounding the attacks in Beleg and Pristina that these victims who were sexually assaulted in this case suffered and the whole series of violent and persecutory acts that they endured. And we have direct evidence of these persecutory and violent acts that these victims endured, at least from two victims, from K14 and K20. And if we draw parallel to the factors that the Chamber took into account when it found that the other crimes -- that discriminatory intent had been established for the other crimes, we can see that these two meet the same requirements that the Chamber found. We know the ethnicity of the victims was Kosovo Albanian and in the case -- and we know that from direct evidence of the victims themselves. We know that the Serb -- that the perpetrators were Serb forces, which is the same as the other acts that the Chamber found to have been carried out as acts of persecution. We also know, and this is an additional factor that the Chamber took into account, at least in the case of K20, that one of the perpetrators made a direct remark to her immediately after she had been gang-raped by Serb soldiers. And we say that this is direct evidence of discriminatory intent. And we know that these victims, in addition to having been sexually assaulted, were also victims of expulsions, of imprisonment in the case of the Beleg victims, of destruction of their homes, and finally they were deported from Kosovo, fulfilling the aims of the JCE to persecute and to forcibly expel the Kosovo Albanian population. Their sexual assaults cannot be disassociated or separated or looked in isolation from the rest of the persecutory acts that they endured. So when we ask Your Honours to look at the context, we are referring to that, to the other violent acts that these same victims endured during the course of the implementation of the campaign by Serb forces. Now, turning to the issue of the foreseeability of these acts, Your Honours, the position we're advancing in our appeal should not be understood as an overly broad interpretation of responsibility under JCE III. In this case we're not speaking, as the Defence suggests, about the general risk of sexual violence during any armed conflict. In fact, we're not even speaking about the risk of sexual violence in any deportation campaign.
