We're talking about a situation where there was a particular common criminal plan which incorporated the use of violence and terror against a targeted population, and what was foreseeable to Djordjevic in those circumstances. We are speaking about the considerably heightened risk of sexual violence happening in the midst of an expulsion campaign where tens of thousands of armed troops are sent into villages and towns and where they come into one-to-one contact with the targeted population and where they're instructed into terrify the targeted population into leaving. And this is the common criminal plan that the Chamber found that Djordjevic had signed up to. In these circumstances, violent crimes against Kosovo Albanians, both men and women alike, were foreseeable consequences of the mass displacement campaign that he and his fellow JCE members implemented. Now, on the issue raised by my colleague about the knowledge of prior crimes or whether these incidents have -- had been reported or not and whether Djordjevic could have had this information available, as I stated in my submissions, it is not a requirement that the -- for a crime to be foreseeable that the accused have prior knowledge that the same types of acts were previously committed. In fact, in the cases that I've listed, and I'm not going to go through the list again, the case law has repeatedly confirmed that awareness of the prevailing contextual factors is sufficient to make, in this case, sexual assault persecutions foreseeable. And I've gone through the different contextual factors that made sexual assaults persecution foreseeable to Djordjevic in this case. So my colleague is simply misstating the relevant jurisprudence when she suggests that there is a requirement of prior knowledge or notice of these crimes. And finally, Your Honours, just to go back to Judge Robinson's and also Judge Agius -- Your Honour Judge Agius' question, in this case -- and I'm going back to the issue of discriminatory intent. In this case, we are not dealing with a case that is entirely based on circumstantial evidence. As I've stated, at least for two victims, K14 and K20, we have direct evidence from the victims themselves of what happened to them and we have direct evidence of the circumstances that surrounded the rapes and the fact that they were targeted because they were Kosovo Albanian women --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's not necessarily direct evidence of discriminatory intent. That's just direct evidence of the event, of the act.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Well -- but, these are factors that the Chamber took into account when assessing the existence or the -- whether the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You did point to one statement which I accept as direct evidence of discriminatory intent where I think the soldier called her -- referred to her ethnicity. But do you have anything more than that?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Well, we know based on the testimonies of the victims what their own ethnicity was, what the ethnicity of the perpetrators was, and we also know the context in which these crimes were committed and all the series of violent acts that they endured, one of which was the sexual assaults during the course of this campaign which was aimed at expelling the population both from Beleg and Pristina. So that evidence is not circumstantial; it's based on the direct testimony of the victims. And so that is the point I'm making.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, incidentally arising from what my colleague Judge Robinson has just mentioned, I notice that when you referred to the event indicating that the same soldier who was guarding one of the girls while all this was happening was the same person that had imprisoned them, et cetera, you failed to give us the exact reference. If you could perhaps give us that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: No problem, Your Honour. The reference is found in -- it's in K20's statement and it's P1279, pages 2 and 4, where the witness herself says when -- in the morning this policeman came to my house and expelled my family, and then she says, I saw the same man guarding the room where I was raped and letting the soldiers in. And this is the direct evidence I'm referring to, Your Honours, and this is the error that we are putting forward that the Chamber made in this case, that it separated the sexual assaults, for example, in the case of K20, from the other persecutory acts that victim endured. In fact, during the course of the same day she was expelled from her home, she was imprisoned, she was separated from -- she and the other women were separated from the men. And the women and girls, a group of them, were taken out that night, sexually assaulted, and the next day the entire village was expelled. And what we're -- and this is direct evidence that comes from the victim herself and she identifies some of the perpetrators that she saw at the scene.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But that is perhaps indicative, as Judge Robinson rightly pointed out, that is perhaps indicative of the Trial Chamber's frame of mind, namely, that insofar as other incidents are concerned, the inference that they arose out of a persecutorial intent were obvious, while in the case of these sexual assaults, the Trial Chamber possibly -- not possibly, obviously thought that there was an equally reasonable inference that could be drawn, namely, that what happened happened independently of any persecutorial -- general persecutorial intent that was prevailing at the time. So this is perhaps territory which is still not sufficiently covered, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, but the only reason the Chamber actually gave in paragraph 1796, and I ask Your Honours to look at that paragraph quite carefully, when they're reasoning why they find that the two sexual -- two rapes that were proven did not amount to persecutions is based on the numbers. They do not give another reason. They just say: Given the limited numbers we can't draw that inference. And as I have already stated in my main submissions, this is -- shouldn't have been a consideration because it's contrary to establish case law of this Appeals Chamber. There is no requirement that a certain number of sexual assaults be proven in order for these to amount to sexual assault. And that is the only reason the Chamber gave to treat these crimes differently from the other -- from the other crimes. And we are submitting that that is wrong in law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Agreed. If -- assuming for argument's sake that you are right, that that argument shouldn't have been made or raised by the Trial Chamber, it still doesn't answer the question that was put, namely, whether the alternative then is that the only inference therefore that could be reached or arrived at is that there was persecutorial intent. So this is what I'm trying to make you understand, that even if you are right, it doesn't mean that the logical consequence of that is that necessarily then there must have been persecutorial intent. It still has to be proved.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Well -- and we say, Your Honours, it was proven, it was established because - and I go again back to my point - that it was established when these acts are looked together with the rest of the violent acts that these victims endured which were considered to be persecutory. And I had pointed out previously that regardless of whether there was a different motive behind the sexual assaults, that does not preclude a finding on discriminatory intent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Just to conclude, Your Honours. It is our submission that no reasonable Trial Chamber could have found that there -- these sexual assaults did not amount to persecutions, and we ask Your Honours to correct the Trial Chamber's errors and confirm that they amounted to persecutions and hold General Djordjevic liable for these crimes under JCE III.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Kravetz. Now, Mr. Djordjevic, lead counsel, but more importantly Mr. Djordjevic, appellant. It is customary for the Appeals Chamber to give an opportunity to the appellant to make a personal address to the Appeals Chamber if you so wish. If you do wish to make a personal statement, you can go ahead and you have ten minutes within which to do so. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE APPELLANT
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you for allowing me to address you. Crimes took place in Kosovo in 1999. I never wanted them, and if I had my time again, I would act very differently. I am deeply sorry for all the victims in Kosovo and the suffering of their families. I apologise unreservedly to the families of all Kosovo Albanian civilians who lost their lives and to those displaced. I truly sympathise with their pain. I hope that the future of the region will be one of peace. I say sorry again today as I apologised during my trial. I hoped to contribute to the process of truth and reconciliation by testifying in my trial for ten days. I wanted to give an open and honest account about my role and about what I knew. Yes, I did learn that crimes had been committed, but only once I was told about the bodies in the Danube river, near Tekija and at Lake Perucac. Yes, I was involved when trucks containing bodies arrived at Batajnica, but I did not know when, where, and how the crimes were committed. I did not oppose the cover-up. I did not take steps to find and prosecute the perpetrators as I should have. I deeply regret this and the fact that I didn't resign immediately. I did not have the strength and power to stand up to the minister. For that, I consider myself responsible. As I said during my trial, I accept that I must pay a price. The reason I did not plead guilty and the reason that I have appealed the trial judgement is because, first, the Prosecution and now the trial judgement say I am responsible for absolutely everything that happened in Kosovo. Honourable Judges, I did play a role and for that I accept that I ought to be punished. But the trial judgement distorts the reality of my role. I beg you to review my role and actions objectively to see that the judgement places too much blame on me. During the war, I was in Belgrade and only on a few occasions I went to Kosovo. I could not issue orders to the head of the MUP staff or its members. It was the minister's staff. They were the focus for the fight against the KLA. I was not a member of the Joint Command in 1999 which also operated in Pristina. Neither did I participate in the making of anti-terrorist plans and their implementation, nor did anyone report to me on these activities. Honourable Judges, as assistant minister and chief of the RJB, I could not give any tasks to any other assistant minister who by minister's decision was in charge of an area of the RJB or asked him to submit reports to me. Once these men were appointed assistant ministers, regardless of rank, they were only answerable to the minister exclusively and only received tasks from the minister. The only superior to us as assistant ministers was the minister himself. Yes, I was involved in the deployment of the reserve formation in Podujevo and the redeployment of some members. But my role in the RJB was removed from day-to-day events in Kosovo. At the time, I thought those decisions made sense because of the threats posed by the KLA and the NATO ground invasion. Your Honours, I say to you frankly, I became marginalised as regards Kosovo. I suppose that my being marginalised made me feel that I could turn away. When I learned that bodies had surfaced in Serbia, I didn't take any measures to find those responsible. I should not have acted like that. I realise that it added to the pain of those who had lost their loved ones. For that, I am truly sorry. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djordjevic. That basically concludes the hearing of the two appeals in this case. On my own behalf and on behalf of my four colleagues, I would like to thank the parties for your absolute co-operation and submissions. I would also like to thank the interpreters who have had a very difficult job and a long day; similarly, the court officers, court staff, our own staff, the IT people, and if I have forgotten anyone, I will say everyone else that was included in the preparation and holding of today's appeal hearing. Thank you for your work and assistance. The Appeals Chamber will issue its judgement in due course. We stand adjourned now. Thank you.
